Measured relations and operator algebras

Almost-connected groups and the solvable radical

Original course text, October 2026. New original expression is public domain (CC0).

Introduction

An amenable group can contain a noncompact solvable part. The positive affine group is an example. For an almost-connected locally compact group, the obstruction lies in the quotient by that part: amenability is equivalent to compactness of the quotient by the solvable radical. We prove this at the full locally compact scope. A closed discrete free subgroup supplies the obstruction; explicit projective matrices make that subgroup visible.

Read Haar averages and compact translation control and Closed subgroups and continuous averaging first. Their full locally compact mean, fixed-point, normal-extension and closed-subgroup proofs are used here. The reduced-word proof for the discrete free group is in Means, Følner sets, and regular representations, Example 4.4.

Throughout, groups are locally compact Hausdorff unless explicitly stated otherwise. No countable base, separability, metrizability or unimodularity is assumed. Section 1A proves the compact-normal quotient input S3 in full, at its stated compact-representation and finite-dimensional Lie prerequisites. Section 1B proves the compact case and the reduction of arbitrary locally compact Lie approximation to the metrizable case, including the quotient topology and metrization proofs. Section 1C constructs the Lie radical and proves the full locally compact radical assertion S1 assuming S2. Sections 1D–1E construct compact conjugation and prove the closed rank-one subgroup input S4 at the explicit root, Lie and geometry prerequisites. The general metrizable Lie-approximation theorem remains unfinished. The other arguments, examples and exercise solutions are given below.

1. Means, components, and the structural inputs

A left invariant mean is a positive unital functional mmm on Haar L∞(G)L^\infty(G)L∞(G) such that m(Lgf)=m(f),Lgf(x)=f(g−1x).(1.1) m(L_gf)=m(f),\qquad L_gf(x)=f(g^{-1}x). \tag{1.1} m(Lg​f)=m(f),Lg​f(x)=f(g−1x).(1.1) The group is amenable when such a mean exists. Use the locally completed Haar convention of the Haar lesson for groups without a sigma-compact hypothesis. Theorem 1.2 there proves equivalence with the uniformly continuous function formulation; Theorem 2.1 proves the compact convex fixed-point criterion. Thus choosing one of these equivalent criteria makes the same definition. This is the complete terminology of Takesaki's Definition XIII.4.2.

Write G∘G^\circG∘ for the identity component. It is closed and characteristic: translations identify all components, and every continuous automorphism fixes the component containing the identity. A group is almost connected when G/G∘G/G^\circG/G∘ is compact. A subgroup is solvable when its algebraic derived series reaches the identity after finitely many steps.

Here are the four structure inputs used in the proof. They concern general locally compact groups or finite-dimensional Lie groups as specified.

Input Exact assertion Source locator
S1 A locally compact group has a largest connected solvable normal subgroup, its radical R=rad⁡GR=\operatorname{rad}GR=radG. It is closed and characteristic. Corollary 1C.9 below, conditional on S2; classical credit: Iwasawa, as recorded in [Rickert], Section 3, pages 439–440.
S2 A connected locally compact group has a compact normal subgroup KKK with Lie quotient. [Rickert], Theorem 1.1, pages 433–434, applied to a connected group; its proof uses the structure theorem of Gleason, Montgomery–Zippin and Yamabe, which is proved in [Tao], Theorem 1.1.17 and Section 1.5.
S3 A quotient of a connected semisimple locally compact group by a compact normal subgroup is semisimple. Theorem 1A.10 below; classical credit: [Rickert], Lemma 3.4, page 440.
S4 A noncompact connected semisimple Lie group has a closed connected Lie subgroup locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R). Theorem 1E.1 below, at the exact root/Lie/geometry providers; classical credit: [Rickert], Lemmas 3.11 and 5.11, pages 442 and 452.

In these assertions, semisimple means that the connected solvable radical is trivial. Section 1A proves S3 by establishing Iwasawa's compact-normal centralizer factorization and the compact-kernel component theorem. Sections 1D–1E construct compact conjugation, a real restricted-weight split triple, a closed adjoint matrix image and its closed inverse-image component in the original group. Section 1C proves S1 using S2 and the explicit finite-dimensional providers. The full local S3 proof does not assert closure of their foundations.

We also use the elementary Lie correspondence between closed subgroups and Lie subalgebras, the exponential chart, and the fact that a connected group locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R) has adjoint quotient PSL2(R)\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)PSL2​(R). The latter follows from integration of the adjoint Lie algebra: the adjoint image is the connected inner automorphism group of sl2(R)\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)sl2​(R), and its kernel is the center. No finiteness assumption on that center is required.

Lemma 1.1 (radical bookkeeping). The radical of G∘G^\circG∘ equals the radical of GGG. The quotient G/RG/RG/R is semisimple. If GGG is almost connected, so is G/RG/RG/R, and (G/R)∘=G∘/R,(G/R)/(G/R)∘≅G/G∘.(1.2) (G/R)^\circ=G^\circ/R,\qquad (G/R)/(G/R)^\circ\cong G/G^\circ. \tag{1.2} (G/R)∘=G∘/R,(G/R)/(G/R)∘≅G/G∘.(1.2)

Proof. Every connected normal solvable subgroup of GGG lies in G∘G^\circG∘, and hence in rad⁡(G∘)\operatorname{rad}(G^\circ)rad(G∘). Conversely the latter radical is characteristic in G∘G^\circG∘, so is normal in GGG. This proves equality.

To check semisimplicity of G/RG/RG/R, let PPP be a connected solvable normal subgroup of that quotient. Replacing it by its closure preserves these three properties: continuity of commutators preserves a finite derived-length bound, and closure preserves connectedness and normality. Its inverse image EEE has connected kernel RRR and connected quotient PPP, so is connected. Indeed, a separation of EEE would separate its connected coset fibers; both pieces would be saturated and their images would separate PPP, since the quotient map is open. The extension of two solvable groups is solvable: after as many derived steps as needed for PPP, the derived subgroup lies in RRR, and then terminates. Thus EEE is connected, solvable and normal in GGG, so E⊂RE\subset RE⊂R. Therefore PPP is trivial.

The component quotient G/G∘G/G^\circG/G∘ is totally disconnected, as proved in Section 1A.4 using Lemma 1A.5. The closed connected subgroup G∘/RG^\circ/RG∘/R of G/RG/RG/R is consequently its identity component: any larger connected component would have a nontrivial connected image in G/G∘G/G^\circG/G∘. This gives (1.2) and the almost-connected conclusion. □\square□

The solvability convention is compatible with closed derived series. If DDD is dense in a group, continuity of commutators puts each successive commutator of D‾\overline DD in the closure of the corresponding derived subgroup of DDD, by induction. A finite termination bound therefore passes to the closure. This is the fact used above and in the Haar lesson's proof that solvable locally compact groups are amenable.

1A. Compact normal quotients and connected solvable lifts

A compact normal subgroup need not be solvable or connected. Lifting a solvable subgroup of the quotient through the whole kernel therefore does not immediately produce a solvable subgroup of the original group. The centralizer supplies the right lift: after replacing the kernel by its compact abelian centre, the finite derived series acquires at most one extra step. The component theorem then produces a connected normal lift.

For a group AAA, define its algebraic derived series by D0A=AD^0A=AD0A=A and Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA]D^{j+1}A=[D^jA,D^jA]Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA], where the brackets mean the subgroup generated by all commutators. “Solvable” means DdA={e}D^dA=\{e\}DdA={e} for some finite integer ddd. A connected solvable normal subgroup need not initially be closed.

We first prove these two mechanisms. The conclusion is Theorem 1A.10, which supplies the compact-normal quotient input used in Proposition 4.1. Section 1C proves existence of the largest solvable radical assuming S2. General Lie approximation remains a separate structure input; Sections 1D–1E prove the closed rank-one subgroup theorem at their exact root, Lie and geometry prerequisites.

The representation prerequisites are finite-dimensional complete reducibility, finite-dimensionality of compact irreducibles, Schur orthogonality, and Peter–Weyl point separation. They apply to arbitrary compact Hausdorff groups. In the finite matrix models we use the closed Lie subgroup theorem, matrix exponentials, and smooth quotients and local sections. These inputs are applied inside finite unitary groups, where their finite-dimensional hypotheses hold.

The classical compact-normal centralizer theorem is due to Kenkichi Iwasawa, as credited in Rickert, Theorem 1.4, printed page 434. Rickert's Lemma 3.4 gives the compact-normal semisimple quotient conclusion. The proof expression below is original and imports no prose from those papers.

1A.4. Components through compact kernels

To lift a connected quotient subgroup, we must know exactly what happens to identity components. We prove the necessary component theorem through compact kernels, including the nonabelian compact-open-subgroup argument. The compact-space lemma below works for every compact Hausdorff space.

Lemma 1A.5 (open maps with connected fibres). If f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y is an open continuous surjection with connected fibres, then the inverse image of every connected subset of YYY is connected.

Proof. For connected B⊂YB\subset YB⊂Y, put E=f−1(B)E=f^{-1}(B)E=f−1(B). The restricted map is open: if UUU is open in XXX, then f(U∩E)=f(U)∩Bf(U\cap E)=f(U)\cap Bf(U∩E)=f(U)∩B. If EEE had a separation into relatively open nonempty parts E1,E2E_1,E_2E1​,E2​, each connected fibre would be wholly in one part. Thus both parts would be saturated, their images would be disjoint nonempty relatively open sets covering BBB, and BBB would be disconnected. □\square□

For any topological group HHH, its identity component H∘H^\circH∘ is closed, since closure preserves connectedness; it is a subgroup, since the continuous image of connected H∘×H∘H^\circ\times H^\circH∘×H∘ under (x,y)↦xy−1(x,y)\mapsto xy^{-1}(x,y)↦xy−1 lies in the identity component; and it is normal, since conjugation fixes the identity and preserves connectedness. Its cosets are all the components by translation.

The group quotient map p:H→H/H∘p:H\to H/H^\circp:H→H/H∘ is open, because p−1(p(U))=UH∘p^{-1}(p(U))=UH^\circp−1(p(U))=UH∘ is open for open UUU. Its fibres are connected. Lemma 1A.5 therefore says that any connected subset of H/H∘H/H^\circH/H∘ has connected inverse image in HHH; that inverse image must lie in a single component, so the subset is a singleton. We have proved H/H∘ is totally disconnected.(1A.16) H/H^\circ\text{ is totally disconnected}. \tag{1A.16} H/H∘ is totally disconnected.(1A.16) This component statement itself does not require local compactness.

We will also use the elementary quotient topology facts. The quotient by a closed subgroup is Hausdorff: the relation x−1y∈Jx^{-1}y\in Jx−1y∈J is closed, and the open surjection p×pp\times pp×p maps its open complement onto the complement of the quotient diagonal. Quotients by closed normal subgroups are topological groups, since the quotient maps and their products are open and hence quotient maps. An open quotient map sends a compact identity neighbourhood to a compact identity neighbourhood, so a quotient of a locally compact group is locally compact. A closed subgroup is locally compact by intersecting a compact neighbourhood with it.

Lemma 1A.6 (compact-space components and clopen neighbourhoods). In a compact Hausdorff space XXX, the component of xxx is the intersection QQQ of all clopen neighbourhoods of xxx. If XXX is totally disconnected, clopen sets form a neighbourhood basis.

Proof. Every connected set through xxx lies in every such clopen set. To prove the reverse inclusion, suppose the compact intersection QQQ were separated into two nonempty compact parts. Normality of a compact Hausdorff space gives disjoint open neighbourhoods U,VU,VU,V of those parts, with x∈Ux\in Ux∈U. The compact complement of U∪VU\cup VU∪V misses QQQ. By the definition of the intersection, each of its points is omitted by some clopen neighbourhood of xxx. A finite subcover of the complements gives a finite intersection DDD of such clopen neighbourhoods with Q⊂D⊂U∪VQ\subset D\subset U\cup VQ⊂D⊂U∪V. Then D∩UD\cap UD∩U is clopen in XXX, contains xxx, and omits the nonempty part of QQQ in VVV, a contradiction. Therefore QQQ is connected and equals the component. Normality used here follows by twice taking finite subcovers of Hausdorff separating neighbourhoods for two disjoint compact closed sets.

If every component is a singleton and OOO is a neighbourhood of xxx, every point of the compact set X∖OX\setminus OX∖O is omitted by a clopen neighbourhood of xxx. Finitely intersecting those neighbourhoods gives a clopen neighbourhood contained in OOO. □\square□

Lemma 1A.7 (van Dantzig, with no commutativity assumption). In every totally disconnected locally compact Hausdorff group TTT, compact open subgroups form a neighbourhood basis at the identity.

Proof. Let WWW be an identity neighbourhood, and choose a compact identity neighbourhood BBB. Take a symmetric open identity neighbourhood VVV with V2⊂W∩int⁡BV^2\subset W\cap\operatorname{int}BV2⊂W∩intB. The inclusion V‾⊂V2\overline V\subset V^2V⊂V2 follows because, for z∈V‾z\in\overline Vz∈V, the open neighbourhood zVzVzV meets VVV, giving z∈VV−1=V2z\in VV^{-1}=V^2z∈VV−1=V2. Thus Q=V‾Q=\overline VQ=V is compact, lies in WWW, and contains the identity in its interior.

This compact space is totally disconnected. Lemma 1A.6 supplies a subset DDD clopen in QQQ, with e∈D⊂int⁡Qe\in D\subset\operatorname{int}Qe∈D⊂intQ. It is compact and also open in TTT: relative openness in QQQ and containment in the interior turn it into an ambient open set.

Use its left stabilizer S={t∈T:tD=D}.(1A.17) S=\{t\in T:tD=D\}. \tag{1A.17} S={t∈T:tD=D}.(1A.17) It is a subgroup. For each d∈Dd\in Dd∈D, continuity of multiplication gives an identity neighbourhood AdA_dAd​ and a neighbourhood OdO_dOd​ of ddd such that AdOd⊂DA_dO_d\subset DAd​Od​⊂D. Finitely many OdO_dOd​'s cover compact DDD. Intersect their identity neighbourhoods and shrink to a symmetric open AAA. Then AD⊂DAD\subset DAD⊂D. Both aD⊂DaD\subset DaD⊂D and a−1D⊂Da^{-1}D\subset Da−1D⊂D hold for a∈Aa\in Aa∈A, so aD=DaD=DaD=D. Hence A⊂SA\subset SA⊂S, and SSS is open.

An open subgroup is closed, because its other cosets are open. Also S⊂DS\subset DS⊂D, since e∈De\in De∈D. Therefore SSS is compact and S⊂WS\subset WS⊂W, proving the assertion. The left stabilizer argument uses no abelian law. □\square□

Corollary 1A.8. A quotient of a totally disconnected locally compact Hausdorff group by a closed normal subgroup is totally disconnected.

Proof. Let r:T→T/Jr:T\to T/Jr:T→T/J be the open quotient map. In the inverse image of any quotient identity neighbourhood, Lemma 1A.7 gives a compact open subgroup SSS. The image r(S)r(S)r(S) is a compact open subgroup in that neighbourhood, and is closed because the quotient is Hausdorff. These clopen neighbourhoods separate the quotient identity from every other point. Translations then exclude every connected set with two different points. □\square□

Theorem 1A.9 (components through a compact kernel). If HHH is locally compact Hausdorff and N⊲HN\lhd HN⊲H is compact, then the quotient map satisfies q(H∘)=(H/N)∘.(1A.18) q(H^\circ)=(H/N)^\circ. \tag{1A.18} q(H∘)=(H/N)∘.(1A.18)

Proof. Set M=q(H∘)M=q(H^\circ)M=q(H∘). Products of a closed set with a compact subgroup are closed, by the argument following (1A.15). Hence qqq is a closed map, so MMM is closed; it is connected and normal as an image of H∘H^\circH∘.

Put T=H/H∘T=H/H^\circT=H/H∘, and let p:H→Tp:H\to Tp:H→T be the quotient map. By (1A.16), TTT is totally disconnected; it is locally compact Hausdorff by the quotient facts proved above. The subgroup p(N)p(N)p(N) is compact and normal. Corollary 1A.8 makes T/p(N)T/p(N)T/p(N) totally disconnected.

1A.5. The compact-normal quotient theorem

1B. Lie approximation: finite kernels and the countability reduction

The general Lie-approximation input S2 concerns a connected locally compact Hausdorff group, which may have no countable neighbourhood base. Two preliminary steps are sometimes hidden when that input is cited: the compact case needs only finitely many representations at each neighbourhood, and the general case can first pass through a compact kernel to a metrizable open subgroup. We prove those steps here. The remaining theorem for metrizable locally compact groups is still an input; the argument below does not replace its no-small-subgroups and Lie-structure proofs.

For classical credit, the finite-kernel argument is the compact Peter–Weyl route to Lie approximation. The countability reduction and the metrization argument are the Kakutani–Gleason part of that route; see Terence Tao, Hilbert's Fifth Problem and Related Topics, Sections 1.4–1.5, especially Theorem 1.4.14, Theorem 1.5.2 and Exercise 1.5.4. The author's freely accessible preliminary version supplies a reading source. We organize the argument around compact fibres and kernel lifting, and give a direct word-cost proof of metrization.

Proposition 1B.1 (the compact case, without a countable base). Let CCC be a compact Hausdorff group and UUU an open neighbourhood of its identity. There is a compact normal subgroup N⊂UN\subset UN⊂U such that C/NC/NC/N is a compact Lie group.

Proof. Peter–Weyl point separation says that, for each x≠ex\ne ex=e, some finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation πx\pi_xπx​ has πx(x)≠I\pi_x(x)\ne Iπx​(x)=I. The open sets {y∈C:πx(y)≠I},x∈C∖U, \{y\in C:\pi_x(y)\ne I\},\qquad x\in C\setminus U, {y∈C:πx​(y)=I},x∈C∖U, cover the compact set C∖UC\setminus UC∖U. Choose a finite subcover, with representations π1,…,πr\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_rπ1​,…,πr​, and take their direct sum π\piπ. Its kernel NNN is closed and normal in CCC, hence compact, and the covering property gives N⊂UN\subset UN⊂U. If U=CU=CU=C, the trivial representation gives the same conclusion with N=CN=CN=C.

The image π(C)⊂U(n)\pi(C)\subset U(n)π(C)⊂U(n) is compact and therefore closed. The closed Lie subgroup theorem makes it a compact Lie group. The induced continuous bijection C/N→π(C)C/N\to\pi(C)C/N→π(C) is a homeomorphism, because its source is compact and its target Hausdorff. This proves the assertion. Only finitely many representations were chosen for this one neighbourhood; no countable family separating all of CCC was assumed. □\square□

We next record the topology needed when a compact kernel is lifted. These facts apply to arbitrary locally compact Hausdorff groups.

Lemma 1B.2 (compact kernels give proper quotient maps). Let HHH be locally compact Hausdorff and N⊲HN\lhd HN⊲H compact. The quotient map q:H→H/Nq:H\to H/Nq:H→H/N is open and closed. The quotient is locally compact Hausdorff, and q−1(B)q^{-1}(B)q−1(B) is compact for every compact subset B⊂H/NB\subset H/NB⊂H/N.

Proof. For open O⊂HO\subset HO⊂H, its saturation ONONON is a union of translates of OOO, hence open; the quotient topology gives openness of qqq. For closed F⊂HF\subset HF⊂H, the product FNFNFN is closed. To verify this without a sequence assumption, let a net finif_i n_ifi​ni​ converge to hhh. Compactness of NNN supplies a subnet with ni→n∈Nn_i\to n\in Nni​→n∈N. Then fi=(fini)ni−1→hn−1∈Ff_i=(f_i n_i)n_i^{-1}\to hn^{-1}\in Ffi​=(fi​ni​)ni−1​→hn−1∈F, so h∈FNh\in FNh∈FN. Thus the saturation of FFF is closed and qqq is closed. Closedness of NNN makes the group quotient Hausdorff: for x∉Nx\notin Nx∈/N, choose an identity neighbourhood WWW with W−1xW∩N=∅W^{-1}xW\cap N=\varnothingW−1xW∩N=∅, and the open images of sufficiently small neighbourhoods of eee and xxx are disjoint. Translation gives separation of any two distinct cosets.

Choose a relatively compact open identity neighbourhood V⊂HV\subset HV⊂H. The compact set q(V‾)q(\overline V)q(V) contains the open neighbourhood q(V)q(V)q(V); thus the quotient is locally compact. Now let BBB be compact. Finitely many translates q(hjV)q(h_jV)q(hj​V) cover BBB. Therefore q−1(B)⊂⋃j=1mhjV‾N. q^{-1}(B)\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^m h_j\overline V N. q−1(B)⊂j=1⋃m​hj​VN. The right side is compact, and the left side is closed because BBB is a compact subset of a Hausdorff quotient. It follows that q−1(B)q^{-1}(B)q−1(B) is compact. □\square□

Lemma 1B.3 (a compact kernel with a countable quotient base). Let GGG be locally compact Hausdorff and UUU an open identity neighbourhood. There are an open sigma-compact subgroup H⊂GH\subset GH⊂G and a compact normal subgroup N⊲HN\lhd HN⊲H such that N⊂UN\subset UN⊂U and H/NH/NH/N has a countable neighbourhood base at its identity. If GGG is connected, H=GH=GH=G.

The intersection is a nonempty compact set, since its closed sets are nested in the compact set W1‾\overline{W_1}W1​​ and contain eee. It lies in UUU. If a,b∈Na,b\in Na,b∈N, then a,b−1∈Wj+1a,b^{-1}\in W_{j+1}a,b−1∈Wj+1​ for every jjj, so ab−1∈Wjab^{-1}\in W_jab−1∈Wj​. Thus NNN is a subgroup. In fact, if O⊂LO\subset LO⊂L is an open identity neighbourhood, its inverse image contains NNN. For completeness, a countable identity base really does supply a metric compatible with the topology; no metrizability hypothesis has been smuggled into Lemma 1B.3.

Lemma 1B.4 (word-cost metrization). A Hausdorff topological group LLL with a countable identity neighbourhood base has a compatible left invariant metric. If LLL is also sigma-compact, it is second countable.

Proof. Refine the given base to symmetric open sets A1⊃A2⊃⋯A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdotsA1​⊃A2​⊃⋯ such that Aj+13⊂AjA_{j+1}^3\subset A_jAj+13​⊂Aj​, and put A0=LA_0=LA0​=L. Let p(x)p(x)p(x) be the infimum of all such costs for words with product xxx; allow the empty word, of cost zero, for eee. Every element has a one-letter word of cost one. Reversing a word and taking inverses preserves its cost, and concatenating words adds costs. Therefore p(x−1)=p(x),p(xy)≤p(x)+p(y).(1B.3) p(x^{-1})=p(x),\qquad p(xy)\leq p(x)+p(y). \tag{1B.3} p(x−1)=p(x),p(xy)≤p(x)+p(y).(1B.3)

The needed lower bound comes from this word estimate: ∑i=1r2−ji<2−n,n≥1⟹x1⋯xr∈An−1.(1B.4) \begin{gathered} \sum_{i=1}^r2^{-j_i}<2^{-n},\quad n\geq1\\ \Longrightarrow\quad x_1\cdots x_r\in A_{n-1}. \end{gathered} \tag{1B.4} i=1∑r​2−ji​<2−n,n≥1⟹x1​⋯xr​∈An−1​.​(1B.4) Prove it by induction on the length rrr, simultaneously for all nnn. For a single letter, its cost is less than 2−n2^{-n}2−n, so j1≥n+1j_1\geq n+1j1​≥n+1 and the assertion holds. For a longer word, write sss for its total cost. Choose the letter at which the running sum first reaches s/2s/2s/2. The words strictly before and strictly after that letter each have total cost at most s/2<2−(n+1)s/2<2^{-(n+1)}s/2<2−(n+1). They have shorter length, so by induction their products lie in AnA_nAn​; an empty side has product e∈Ane\in A_ne∈An​. The middle letter belongs to AnA_nAn​ as well, because its cost is at most s<2−ns<2^{-n}s<2−n. The full product lies in An3⊂An−1A_n^3\subset A_{n-1}An3​⊂An−1​. This proves (1B.4); it does not rearrange the letters, which matters in a noncommutative group.

If p(x)<2−np(x)<2^{-n}p(x)<2−n, an approximating word of cost less than 2−n2^{-n}2−n shows x∈An−1x\in A_{n-1}x∈An−1​. If x∈Anx\in A_nx∈An​, its one-letter word gives p(x)≤2−np(x)\leq2^{-n}p(x)≤2−n. Hence p(x)=0p(x)=0p(x)=0 forces x=ex=ex=e, and d(x,y)=p(x−1y) d(x,y)=p(x^{-1}y) d(x,y)=p(x−1y) is a metric by (1B.3), invariant under common left multiplication. The two inclusions just proved show that its balls and the sets AjA_jAj​ give the same neighbourhood system at eee, and translation gives the same topology everywhere.

If LLL is sigma-compact, write it as a countable union of compact sets. Each compact metric space has a countable dense subset: for each integer m≥1m\geq1m≥1, take the centres of a finite cover by balls of radius 1/m1/m1/m, and unite those finite sets. Their union over the compact covering sets is countable and dense in LLL. A metric space with a countable dense subset has the countable base of balls with those centres and positive rational radii. Thus LLL is second countable. □\square□

Proposition 1B.5 (the exact reduction for S2). Suppose the following metrizable theorem is available: every metrizable locally compact Hausdorff group LLL, and every open identity neighbourhood O⊂LO\subset LO⊂L, admit an open subgroup L′⊂LL'\subset LL′⊂L and a compact normal subgroup B⊲L′B\lhd L'B⊲L′, with B⊂OB\subset OB⊂O and L′/BL'/BL′/B a Lie group. Then the same assertion holds for every locally compact Hausdorff group GGG. For connected GGG, the resulting open subgroup is all of GGG, giving exactly S2.

Proof. Fix an open identity neighbourhood U⊂GU\subset GU⊂G. Use Lemma 1B.3 to obtain HHH and N⊂UN\subset UN⊂U, and let q:H→L=H/Nq:H\to L=H/Nq:H→L=H/N. Lemma 1B.4 makes LLL metrizable. There is an open identity neighbourhood W⊂HW\subset HW⊂H with WN⊂UWN\subset UWN⊂U. To verify this shrinking, for each n∈Nn\in Nn∈N, continuity gives an identity neighbourhood WnW_nWn​ and a neighbourhood TnT_nTn​ of nnn with WnTn⊂UW_nT_n\subset UWn​Tn​⊂U. Take a finite cover of the compact set NNN by these TnT_nTn​, and intersect the corresponding WnW_nWn​.

The set O=q(W)O=q(W)O=q(W) is an open identity neighbourhood in LLL, and q−1(O)=WN⊂Uq^{-1}(O)=WN\subset Uq−1(O)=WN⊂U. Apply the stated metrizable theorem to obtain L′L'L′ and BBB. Set G′=q−1(L′),K=q−1(B). G'=q^{-1}(L'),\qquad K=q^{-1}(B). G′=q−1(L′),K=q−1(B). Then G′G'G′ is open in HHH, hence in GGG; KKK is normal in G′G'G′, is contained in UUU, and is compact by Lemma 1B.2. The surjective composite G′→L′→L′/BG'\to L'\to L'/BG′→L′→L′/B is continuous and open, with kernel KKK. It consequently induces a topological group isomorphism G′/K≅L′/BG'/K\cong L'/BG′/K≅L′/B, a Lie group. If GGG is connected, G′=GG'=GG′=G because an open subgroup is closed. □\square□

This reduction retains the arbitrary locally compact scope. It leaves a specific mathematical obligation: the metrizable theorem in Proposition 1B.5. In particular, a proof only for compact groups, or an invocation that a no-small-subgroups group is Lie without its proof, does not finish S2.

Exercise 1B.1 (what a finite compact quotient can see). Level 2. Let III be uncountable, let C=TIC=\mathbb T^IC=TI with the product topology, and let UUU be any open identity neighbourhood. Prove directly that there is a compact normal subgroup N⊂UN\subset UN⊂U with C/NC/NC/N a finite-dimensional torus. Prove also that CCC has no countable identity neighbourhood base. Explain why these two facts are consistent with Proposition 1B.1.

Solution. Choose a basic product neighbourhood inside UUU. It restricts only finitely many coordinates, say those in F⊂IF\subset IF⊂I, and each restriction contains 111. The subgroup N={z∈TI:zi=1 for every i∈F} N=\{z\in\mathbb T^I:z_i=1\text{ for every }i\in F\} N={z∈TI:zi​=1 for every i∈F} is a closed subgroup of the compact Hausdorff product, hence compact, and it is normal because the product is abelian. It lies in the chosen product neighbourhood. Projection onto FFF is a continuous surjection with kernel NNN; compactness and Hausdorffness identify C/NC/NC/N topologically with TF\mathbb T^FTF.

Suppose that O1,O2,…O_1,O_2,\ldotsO1​,O2​,… were a countable identity base. For each nnn, choose a basic product neighbourhood Bn⊂OnB_n\subset O_nBn​⊂On​, restricting a finite set FnF_nFn​. Their union is countable, so choose i∈I∖⋃nFni\in I\setminus\bigcup_nF_ni∈I∖⋃n​Fn​. Let WWW be the identity neighbourhood requiring ziz_izi​ to lie in a fixed proper open arc around 111. A base would give On⊂WO_n\subset WOn​⊂W for some nnn, and then Bn⊂WB_n\subset WBn​⊂W. But BnB_nBn​ leaves coordinate iii unrestricted, a contradiction. Each neighbourhood permits a finite Lie quotient, while different neighbourhoods may require different finite coordinate sets; the proposition does not assert a countable family sufficient for every neighbourhood.

Exercise 1B.2 (why the open subgroup is part of the statement). Level 1. Let DDD be an uncountable discrete group and G=R×DG=\mathbb R\times DG=R×D, with the product topology. Prove that GGG is locally compact Hausdorff but is not sigma-compact. For V=(−1,1)×{e}V=(-1,1)\times\{e\}V=(−1,1)×{e}, identify the subgroup H=⋃m≥1VmH=\bigcup_{m\geq1}V^mH=⋃m≥1​Vm in Lemma 1B.3. Prove that the connectedness qualification at the end of Proposition 1B.5 is exactly what removes this proper open subgroup.

Solution. Each point has a neighbourhood with compact closure, namely an interval with compact closure times a singleton of DDD; the product is Hausdorff. A compact subset of GGG projects to a compact subset of the discrete space DDD, hence to a finite set. A countable union of compact subsets therefore projects to at most countably many elements of DDD, so it cannot cover GGG.

Addition in the real coordinate gives Vm=(−m,m)×{e}V^m=(-m,m)\times\{e\}Vm=(−m,m)×{e} and H=R×{e}H=\mathbb R\times\{e\}H=R×{e}. This is a proper open and closed sigma-compact subgroup. Every connected subset containing the identity has constant projection to DDD, and R×{e}\mathbb R\times\{e\}R×{e} itself is connected; thus it is G∘G^\circG∘. The construction cannot force H=GH=GH=G here. For a connected group, however, the complement of any proper open subgroup is a nonempty union of open cosets, giving a separation. This is the step that forces H=GH=GH=G, and subsequently G′=GG'=GG′=G, in the connected case.

1C. Constructing the closed solvable radical

The full locally compact radical requires a common finite bound, not just solvability of each subgroup separately. We first establish the unrestricted finite-dimensional Lie-group contract, including nonlinear groups and infinite centres. Then one compact Lie quotient supplies the same bound for every connected solvable normal subgroup of the original group. This proves S1 at the Lie-approximation input S2; the remaining metrizable Gleason–Yamabe theorem in Proposition 1B.5 is still an explicit prerequisite.

The finite-dimensional prerequisites are the closed subgroup theorem, connected immersed integration, and the smoothly generated subgroup proof. Covering groups, unrestricted-target integration, the adjoint differential and the compact Lie-algebra structure are proved in Compact Lie groups, their Lie algebras and the adjoint representation, Theorems 1.2 and 3.2. Peter–Weyl point separation is the arbitrary compact Hausdorff theorem already linked in Section 1A. Ordinary inverse-function calculus and exponential neighbourhoods retain their stated finite-dimensional scope.

The radical and quotient algebra assertions can also be compared with Etingof, Section 16.1. The locally compact radical is classically attributed to Iwasawa in Rickert, Section 3, printed pages 439–440.

1C.1. The finite-dimensional contract and radical ideal

Let GGG be a connected finite-dimensional real Lie group, with the usual Hausdorff, second-countable manifold convention, and let g=TeG\mathfrak g=T_eGg=Te​G. There is no assumption of linearity, simple connectivity, compactness, or finite centre.

For an abstract subgroup AAA, its algebraic derived series is

D0A=A,Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA], D^0A=A,\qquad D^{j+1}A=[D^jA,D^jA], D0A=A,Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA],

DLie0a=a,DLiej+1a=span⁡R{[X,Y]:X,Y∈DLieja}. \begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^0\mathfrak a&=\mathfrak a,\\ D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^{j+1}\mathfrak a&=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R} \{[X,Y]:X,Y\in D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^j\mathfrak a\}. \end{aligned} DLie0​aDLiej+1​a​=a,=spanR​{[X,Y]:X,Y∈DLiej​a}.​

Solvability means that the appropriate series vanishes after finitely many steps. Group characteristicness here concerns continuous group automorphisms, matching the convention of this lesson. No assertion about discontinuous abstract automorphisms is needed.

Theorem 1C.5. The Lie algebra g\mathfrak gg has a largest solvable ideal r\mathfrak rr. Its unique connected immersed integration is a subgroup R⊂GR\subset GR⊂G such that:

  1. RRR is closed, connected, normal and embedded, and Lie⁡(R)=r\operatorname{Lie}(R)=\mathfrak rLie(R)=r.
  2. RRR is algebraically solvable, with the uniform bound Ddim⁡rR={e}.(1C.1) D^{\dim\mathfrak r}R=\{e\}. \tag{1C.1} DdimrR={e}.(1C.1) In dimension zero this says R={e}R=\{e\}R={e}.
  3. Every connected algebraically solvable normal subgroup P⊂GP\subset GP⊂G, even one that is not closed, is contained in RRR.
  4. RRR is characteristic under continuous automorphisms.

The bound (1C.1) is a convenient upper bound, not a claim about minimal derived length or equality with the Lie-algebra derived length.

Lemma 1C.1. A finite-dimensional real Lie algebra has a largest solvable ideal r\mathfrak rr, preserved by every Lie-algebra automorphism. The quotient g/r\mathfrak g/\mathfrak rg/r has no nonzero solvable ideal, and in particular has zero centre.

Proof. Subalgebras inherit solvability by containment of derived terms, and quotients inherit it by taking their images. An extension of solvable Lie algebras is solvable: if I◃aI\triangleleft\mathfrak aI◃a, DLieuI=0D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^u I=0DLieu​I=0, and DLiev(a/I)=0D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^v(\mathfrak a/I)=0DLiev​(a/I)=0, then DLieva⊂ID_{\mathrm{Lie}}^v\mathfrak a\subset IDLiev​a⊂I, so DLieu+va=0D_{\mathrm{Lie}}^{u+v}\mathfrak a=0DLieu+v​a=0.

For solvable ideals I,JI,JI,J, the ideal I+JI+JI+J is an extension of III by J/(I∩J)J/(I\cap J)J/(I∩J), hence is solvable. Any finite sum is therefore solvable. The sum of all solvable ideals is already a finite sum: choose a basis of this finite-dimensional sum, and collect the finitely many ideals needed to express its finitely many basis vectors. This sum r\mathfrak rr is consequently solvable, is an ideal, and contains every solvable ideal. Automorphisms permute those ideals, hence preserve r\mathfrak rr.

The inverse image of any solvable ideal in g/r\mathfrak g/\mathfrak rg/r would be a solvable extension of r\mathfrak rr. Maximality puts that inverse image inside r\mathfrak rr, so the quotient ideal is zero. Its centre is an abelian ideal and must therefore be zero. □\square□

This is exactly the semisimple-quotient property used in the group proof; it requires no structure theorem for semisimple groups.

1C.2. Lie solvability and finite group bounds

1C.3. The adjoint quotient makes the radical closed

Proof of Theorem 1C.5. Let r\mathfrak rr be from Lemma 1C.1. Its automorphism invariance makes it invariant under every Ad⁡g\operatorname{Ad}_gAdg​. Thus on V=g/rV=\mathfrak g/\mathfrak rV=g/r there is a smooth homomorphism

Its Lie algebra is ker⁡dΘe\ker d\Theta_ekerdΘe​: by the closed subgroup theorem, X∈Lie⁡(K)X\in\operatorname{Lie}(K)X∈Lie(K) exactly when Θ(exp⁡(tX))=I\Theta(\exp(tX))=IΘ(exp(tX))=I for all ttt; intertwining exponentials makes that equivalent to dΘe(X)=0d\Theta_e(X)=0dΘe​(X)=0.

dΘe(X)(Y+r)=[X,Y]+r. d\Theta_e(X)(Y+\mathfrak r)=[X,Y]+\mathfrak r. dΘe​(X)(Y+r)=[X,Y]+r.

Lie⁡(K)=r.(1C.5) \operatorname{Lie}(K)=\mathfrak r. \tag{1C.5} Lie(K)=r.(1C.5)

Set R=K∘R=K^\circR=K∘. Components are closed, and KKK is closed in GGG, so RRR is closed in GGG. Conjugation preserves the identity component, making RRR normal. The identity component of a Lie group has the same Lie algebra as that group; hence Lie⁡(R)=r\operatorname{Lie}(R)=\mathfrak rLie(R)=r. It is connected and embedded.

Every exp⁡(tX)\exp(tX)exp(tX), X∈rX\in\mathfrak rX∈r, lies in RRR, and these one-parameter subgroups generate RRR. They also generate the unique connected immersed integration of r\mathfrak rr, by its intrinsic exponential neighbourhoods. The two subgroups therefore coincide, and RRR supplies the embedded structure. This establishes closedness rather than assuming it when integrating the ideal. The matrix target GL(V)GL(V)GL(V) does not require a faithful representation of GGG.

Apply Lemma 1C.4 to RRR to obtain the algebraic bound (1C.1).

For maximality, let P⊂GP\subset GP⊂G be connected, algebraically solvable and normal, with some finite bound DdP={e}D^dP=\{e\}DdP={e}. The closure H=P‾H=\overline PH=P is connected and normal and has that same bound by Lemma 1C.2. It is a closed Lie subgroup. Lemma 1C.3 makes h=Lie⁡(H)\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)h=Lie(H) a solvable ideal of g\mathfrak gg, so h⊂r\mathfrak h\subset\mathfrak rh⊂r. Its exponentials agree with those in GGG and lie in RRR. They generate connected HHH, so P⊂H⊂RP\subset H\subset RP⊂H⊂R.

Finally, a continuous automorphism α\alphaα takes RRR to a connected algebraically solvable normal subgroup. Maximality gives α(R)⊂R\alpha(R)\subset Rα(R)⊂R. Applying the same fact to α−1\alpha^{-1}α−1 yields equality. This proves characteristicness without an extra automatic-smoothness theorem for α\alphaα. □\square□

If r=g\mathfrak r=\mathfrak gr=g, then V=0V=0V=0, Θ\ThetaΘ has trivial target, and R=GR=GR=G; Lemma 1C.4 still gives finite algebraic solvability. If r=0\mathfrak r=0r=0, KKK has zero-dimensional Lie algebra but may be an infinite discrete subgroup; K∘={e}K^\circ=\{e\}K∘={e}. A large discrete centre creates no exception.

An alternative closedness argument first applies Lemma 1C.4 to the immersed radical with its intrinsic Lie topology. Its closure is connected, normal and algebraically solvable, so Lemma 1C.3 gives a solvable ideal containing r\mathfrak rr. Equality of Lie algebras and connected exponential generation then force equality with its closure. The kernel construction gives the closed subgroup directly.

1C.4. An infinite centre outside the connected radical

Take G=SL2(R)~G=\widetilde{SL_2(\mathbb R)}G=SL2​(R)​, the connected universal covering Lie group. Its centre is infinite, but its radical is trivial.

Indeed any M∈SL2(R)M\in SL_2(\mathbb R)M∈SL2​(R) has the unique smooth factorisation

M=Q(rs0r−1),Q∈SO(2),r>0,s∈R. \begin{gathered} M=Q\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\\ Q\in SO(2),\quad r>0,\quad s\in\mathbb R. \end{gathered} M=Q(r0​sr−1​),Q∈SO(2),r>0,s∈R.​

To obtain it, let v≠0v\ne0v=0 be the first column, take r=∥v∥r=\|v\|r=∥v∥, and choose QQQ with columns v/rv/rv/r and its positive quarter-turn. Multiplying by Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 gives the displayed upper triangular matrix; determinant one fixes its second diagonal entry. The formula is a smooth inverse, so SL2(R)SL_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R) is diffeomorphic to SO(2)×(0,∞)×RSO(2)\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb RSO(2)×(0,∞)×R. The last two factors contract, and the circle SO(2)SO(2)SO(2) has fundamental group Z\mathbb ZZ. Explicitly, lift a circle loop under t↦(cos⁡(2πt),sin⁡(2πt))t\mapsto(\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))t↦(cos(2πt),sin(2πt)): its endpoint is an integer, homotopy lifting preserves that integer, and its lift deforms to the straight path with that endpoint.

The covering homomorphism therefore has a discrete kernel isomorphic to Z\mathbb ZZ. It is central: for any kernel element zzz, the map g↦gzg−1g\mapsto gzg^{-1}g↦gzg−1 from connected GGG into the discrete kernel is constant and equals zzz at the identity.

The Lie algebra sl2(R)\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)sl2​(R), however, is simple. In its standard basis E,F,HE,F,HE,F,H,

[H,E]=2E,[H,F]=−2F,[E,F]=H. \begin{aligned} [H,E]&=2E,\\ [H,F]&=-2F,\\ [E,F]&=H. \end{aligned} [H,E][H,F][E,F]​=2E,=−2F,=H.​

Any nonzero ideal is stable under ad⁡H\operatorname{ad}HadH. Polynomial projections onto its distinct eigenspaces of eigenvalues 2,−2,02,-2,02,−2,0 isolate a nonzero multiple of at least one of E,F,HE,F,HE,F,H in that ideal. Bracketing with the other basis vectors gives all three. The algebra has no nonzero proper ideal and is not solvable, since its commutator is the whole algebra. Its radical is zero, so Theorem 1C.5 gives R={e}R=\{e\}R={e}. An infinite discrete abelian central subgroup is not part of the connected radical.

1C.5. Two diagnostics for nonclosed subgroups

Exercise 1C.1 (a solvable immersed normal subgroup need not be closed). Level 2.

Let α∉Q\alpha\notin\mathbb Qα∈/Q, T2=R2/Z2T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2T2=R2/Z2, and

Nα={(t,αt)+Z2:t∈R}. N_\alpha=\{(t,\alpha t)+\mathbb Z^2:t\in\mathbb R\}. Nα​={(t,αt)+Z2:t∈R}.

Prove that NαN_\alphaNα​ is proper, dense, connected, abelian and normal. Find the radical of T2T^2T2, and explain why maximality and the universal cover are essential to the preceding proof.

Solution. The map from R\mathbb RR is a smooth homomorphism. If (t,αt)∈Z2(t,\alpha t)\in\mathbb Z^2(t,αt)∈Z2, irrationality forces t=0t=0t=0, so it is injective, giving a connected immersed subgroup with one-dimensional intrinsic Lie algebra. The ambient group is abelian, giving abelianity and normality.

At integer parameters its image contains (0,αn)+Z2(0,\alpha n)+\mathbb Z^2(0,αn)+Z2. The irrational rotation subgroup is dense in the circle: among arbitrarily many distinct subgroup points, division into short equal intervals gives two arbitrarily close points. Their difference, changing sign if necessary, has representative 0<δ<ε0<\delta<\varepsilon0<δ<ε. Its multiples 0,δ,…,⌊1/δ⌋δ0,\delta,\ldots,\lfloor1/\delta\rfloor\delta0,δ,…,⌊1/δ⌋δ approximate every circle point within δ\deltaδ. Thus the closure contains the vertical circle. Since the parameter t=xt=xt=x supplies any first coordinate x+Zx+\mathbb Zx+Z, addition of that vertical circle proves Nα‾=T2\overline{N_\alpha}=T^2Nα​​=T2.

The point (0,α/2)+Z2(0,\alpha/2)+\mathbb Z^2(0,α/2)+Z2 is absent. Membership would force t∈Zt\in\mathbb Zt∈Z and α(t−12)∈Z\alpha(t-\tfrac12)\in\mathbb Zα(t−21​)∈Z, impossible for irrational α\alphaα. Hence the subgroup is proper and nonclosed.

The Lie algebra of T2T^2T2 is abelian, so its radical is all of R2\mathbb R^2R2; the group radical is T2T^2T2. The line R(1,α)\mathbb R(1,\alpha)R(1,α) is a solvable ideal but is not maximal. This disproves closedness for an arbitrary solvable ideal's integration. The radical kernel argument uses the maximal ideal and the zero centre of its semisimple quotient.

There is no nonzero continuous homomorphism T2→(R,+)T^2\to(\mathbb R,+)T2→(R,+): its image is compact, whereas any nonzero subgroup of R\mathbb RR is unbounded. Yet its Lie algebra has nonzero real characters. Lemma 1C.4 integrates them on the simply connected cover R2\mathbb R^2R2; they need not descend to the torus. □\square□

Exercise 1C.2 (a nonlinear solvable group with nonclosed derived subgroup). Level 3.

This is a classical Heisenberg central-quotient diagnostic; compare Etingof, Exercise 15.7(ii). The cocycle below specifies the exact group law, and the solution proves nonlinearity.

Keep α\alphaα irrational and put v=(1,α)v=(1,\alpha)v=(1,α). On R2×T2\mathbb R^2\times T^2R2×T2 define

(x,y,z)(x′,y′,z′)=(x+x′,y+y′,z+z′+xy′v),(1C.6) \begin{aligned} (x,y,z)(x',y',z')&=\\ &\hspace{-4em}(x+x',y+y',z+z'+xy'v), \end{aligned} \tag{1C.6} (x,y,z)(x′,y′,z′)​=(x+x′,y+y′,z+z′+xy′v),​(1C.6)

xy′+(x+x′)y′′=x′y′′+x(y′+y′′). xy'+(x+x')y''=x'y''+x(y'+y''). xy′+(x+x′)y′′=x′y′′+x(y′+y′′).

The identity is (0,0,0)(0,0,0)(0,0,0); the inverse is (−x,−y,−z+xyv)(-x,-y,-z+xyv)(−x,−y,−z+xyv), which gives the identity on both sides. The underlying manifold is connected, Hausdorff and second countable, of dimension four.

Direct multiplication gives

[(x,y,z),(x′,y′,z′)]=(0,0,(xy′−x′y)v).(1C.7) [(x,y,z),(x',y',z')]=(0,0,(xy'-x'y)v). \tag{1C.7} [(x,y,z),(x′,y′,z′)]=(0,0,(xy′−x′y)v).(1C.7)

D1Gα={0}×{0}×Nα,D2Gα={e}. D^1G_\alpha=\{0\}\times\{0\}\times N_\alpha,\qquad D^2G_\alpha=\{e\}. D1Gα​={0}×{0}×Nα​,D2Gα​={e}.

The first derived subgroup is nontrivial, central and nonclosed, with closure the central torus, by Exercise 1C.1. The group has algebraic derived length exactly two.

In Lie-algebra coordinate basis X,Y,Z1,Z2X,Y,Z_1,Z_2X,Y,Z1​,Z2​, differentiation gives

1C.6. One compact kernel gives a uniform bound

Lemma 1C.6 (connected derived subgroups and closure). Let PPP be a subgroup of a Hausdorff topological group HHH, with its subspace topology, and take all closures in HHH. If PPP is connected, every algebraic derived subgroup DjPD^jPDjP is connected. For any integer d≥0d\geq0d≥0, DdP={e}D^dP=\{e\}DdP={e} implies DdP‾={e}D^d\overline P=\{e\}DdP={e}.

Proof. The commutator map P×P→PP\times P\to PP×P→P is continuous, so its image is connected and contains the identity. The subgroup generated by this image is the increasing union of finite products of the image and its inverse. Each such product is a continuous image of a connected finite product and contains the identity. The union is connected. Iteration proves connectedness of every DjPD^jPDjP.

For the closure assertion, commutator continuity gives [A‾,A‾]⊂[A,A]‾ [\overline A,\overline A]\subset\overline{[A,A]} [A,A]⊂[A,A]​ for every subgroup AAA: approximate each pair by a product net from A×AA\times AA×A, and then take finite products and inverses of the resulting commutators. Induction gives DjP‾⊂DjP‾D^j\overline P\subset\overline{D^jP}DjP⊂DjP. At j=dj=dj=d the right side is {e}\{e\}{e}, since the ambient group is Hausdorff. Thus the same finite bound passes to the closure. □\square□

If DdJ={e}D^dJ=\{e\}DdJ={e}, then wdw_dwd​ is identically eee on J2dJ^{2^d}J2d. Evaluate it at xi=exp⁡(tiXi)x_i=\exp(t_iX_i)xi​=exp(ti​Xi​). Induction on the balanced expressions therefore gives vj(X1,…,X2j)v_j(X_1,\ldots,X_{2^j})vj​(X1​,…,X2j​) as the coefficient of t1⋯t2jt_1\cdots t_{2^j}t1​⋯t2j​ in wj−Iw_j-Iwj​−I. One can track this coefficient exactly: each expression is the identity when any of its variables is zero, so every nonconstant term contains every variable in its block; in the next commutator the term containing each variable once is precisely the commutator of the two corresponding coefficients. The identity for wdw_dwd​ makes vd=0v_d=0vd​=0. Bilinearity of the Lie bracket shows inductively that the values of vjv_jvj​ span DjjD^j\mathfrak jDjj, so Ddj=0D^d\mathfrak j=0Ddj=0.

The finite-dimensional compact Lie-algebra structure theorem gives j=z⊕s\mathfrak j=\mathfrak z\oplus\mathfrak sj=z⊕s, with z\mathfrak zz central and s\mathfrak ss semisimple. Theorem 1C.8 (one compact-kernel quotient gives a uniform radical bound). Let GGG be connected locally compact Hausdorff. Suppose K⊲GK\lhd GK⊲G is compact, L=G/KL=G/KL=G/K is a Lie group, and its Lie radical RLR_LRL​ has algebraic derived length at most ddd. Then every connected algebraically solvable normal subgroup P⊲GP\lhd GP⊲G, closed or not, has derived length at most d+1d+1d+1. The closure of the union of all such PPP is the largest connected solvable normal subgroup of GGG; it is closed and characteristic.

Proof. Let q:G→Lq:G\to Lq:G→L. The image q(P)q(P)q(P) is connected, solvable and normal. Its closure has these properties by Lemma 1C.6 and commutator continuity; the Lie radical contract puts it in RLR_LRL​. Therefore DdP⊂K. D^dP\subset K. DdP⊂K. By Lemma 1C.6 the subgroup DdPD^dPDdP is connected, and its closure CCC is connected and solvable. It is compact because it is closed inside the compact kernel KKK. Lemma 1C.7 makes CCC abelian, whence Dd+1P={e}D^{d+1}P=\{e\}Dd+1P={e}. The bound depends only on the one Lie quotient, not on the initially unknown derived length of PPP.

If P,QP,QP,Q are two connected solvable normal subgroups, PQPQPQ is a normal subgroup and is connected as the continuous image of P×QP\times QP×Q. It is algebraically solvable: P⊲PQP\lhd PQP⊲PQ, the quotient is an image of QQQ, and successive derived steps first enter PPP and then terminate. Thus PQPQPQ belongs to the same family. This family is directed by inclusion.

Let AAA be its union. Directedness makes AAA a subgroup; it is normal, and it is connected because its connected constituent subgroups all contain eee. It satisfies Dd+1A={e}D^{d+1}A=\{e\}Dd+1A={e}. To check this without an illicit bound depending on the number of factors, any element of DjAD^jADjA is a finite expression of products, inverses and nested commutators of elements of AAA. Those finitely many elements lie together in one constituent subgroup PPP, by directedness, so that expression lies in DjPD^jPDjP. This proves DjA⊂⋃PDjPD^jA\subset\bigcup_P D^jPDjA⊂⋃P​DjP; the opposite inclusion is immediate. The uniform bound already proved for every PPP now gives termination for AAA.

Set R=A‾R=\overline AR=A. It is closed, connected and normal, and Lemma 1C.6 preserves the bound Dd+1R={e}D^{d+1}R=\{e\}Dd+1R={e}. It contains every connected solvable normal subgroup by construction, so it is the largest. Every topological automorphism of GGG permutes that defining family and preserves closure, hence fixes RRR. Thus RRR is characteristic. □\square□

Corollary 1C.9 (the full locally compact radical, assuming S2). Assuming S2, every locally compact Hausdorff group has a closed characteristic largest connected algebraically solvable normal subgroup.

Proof. The identity component G∘G^\circG∘ is closed, hence locally compact Hausdorff, and characteristic in GGG. By S2 it has one compact normal kernel with Lie quotient, whose radical is supplied by Theorem 1C.5, so Theorem 1C.8 produces its radical R0R_0R0​. Characteristicity of R0R_0R0​ in G∘G^\circG∘, and of G∘G^\circG∘ in GGG, makes R0R_0R0​ normal and characteristic in GGG. It is closed in GGG because both inclusions are closed. Every connected solvable normal subgroup of GGG lies in G∘G^\circG∘ and is normal there, so it lies in R0R_0R0​. Conversely R0R_0R0​ itself is connected, solvable and normal in GGG. These two inclusions establish the largest-subgroup assertion for GGG, with no countability or almost-connected assumption. □\square□

Exercise 1C.3 (a compact kernel need not be solvable). Level 2. Suppose GGG is connected, K⊲GK\lhd GK⊲G compact and G/KG/KG/K has trivial Lie radical. Show that every connected solvable normal subgroup of GGG is abelian and lies in KKK. Explain why the conclusion does not make KKK solvable.

Solution. In Theorem 1C.8 use d=0d=0d=0, with the convention D0P=PD^0P=PD0P=P. The image of PPP lies in the trivial radical, so P⊂KP\subset KP⊂K; its compact connected solvable closure is abelian by Lemma 1C.7, and therefore PPP is abelian. For example, take G=K=SU(2)G=K=SU(2)G=K=SU(2), so the quotient is trivial. Matrices in SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) have the form (zw−w‾z‾),∣z∣2+∣w∣2=1. \begin{pmatrix}z&w\\-\overline w&\overline z\end{pmatrix}, \qquad |z|^2+|w|^2=1. (z−w​wz​),∣z∣2+∣w∣2=1. This identifies the group with the connected sphere S3S^3S3. The matrices obtained from (z,w)=(i,0)(z,w)=(i,0)(z,w)=(i,0) and (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) anticommute, so the group is nonabelian. If it were solvable, Lemma 1C.7 would make it abelian, a contradiction. The claim concerns the connected solvable normal subgroups, not every subgroup of the compact kernel.

Exercise 1C.4 (why the common bound matters). Level 2. Let P,Q⊲GP,Q\lhd GP,Q⊲G be connected solvable normal subgroups with respective derived lengths a,ba,ba,b. Prove Da+b(PQ)={e}D^{a+b}(PQ)=\{e\}Da+b(PQ)={e}. If GGG has the quotient in Theorem 1C.8 with radical length ddd, prove the stronger bound Dd+1(PQ)={e}D^{d+1}(PQ)=\{e\}Dd+1(PQ)={e}, independent of a+ba+ba+b, and identify exactly why that independence is needed for the full radical.

Solution. The quotient PQ/PPQ/PPQ/P is an image of QQQ, so Db(PQ)⊂PD^b(PQ)\subset PDb(PQ)⊂P. Another aaa steps terminate, giving the first bound. Normality makes PQPQPQ a subgroup, and connectedness follows from multiplication on P×QP\times QP×Q; thus PQPQPQ is a member of the family covered by Theorem 1C.8, giving the uniform d+1d+1d+1 bound. An unbounded collection of terminating derived lengths does not provide a single finite bound on its union. The compact-kernel argument supplies one bound for all members and all finite products, which is precisely what permits the passage to the directed union and then its closure.

1D. Constructing a compact conjugation from root spaces

The closed subgroup proof in Section 1E needs a positive inner product compatible with the Lie bracket. We construct it here on every complex semisimple algebra. The compact conjugation is obtained on the actual algebra, so assigning values to simple generators will not conceal an unproved presentation theorem.

The root-production prerequisite RP is Theorem 12.1 and its complete proof, Sections 12.2–12.10, in Symmetric Lie algebras and Hermitian symmetric spaces. Its complete reducibility proof uses the operator Casimir and the first Whitehead lemma before any compact real form is available. We use its exact assertion as follows.

The Killing form B=BCB=B_{\mathbb C}B=BC​ is nondegenerate, its restriction to hR\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}hR​ is real positive definite, and the root-space pairings are nondegenerate between opposite roots and zero for other pairs. p,q≥0,β(hα)=p−q,n=p+q.(1D.4) p,q\geq0,\qquad \beta(h_\alpha)=p-q, \qquad n=p+q. \tag{1D.4} p,q≥0,β(hα​)=p−q,n=p+q.(1D.4)

Theorem 1D.1 (compact conjugation). At the root-production input RP above, every finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra has a conjugate-linear involutive Lie automorphism τ\tauτ for which q(X,Y)=−BC(X,τY)q(X,Y)=-B_{\mathbb C}(X,\tau Y)q(X,Y)=−BC​(X,τY) is positive Hermitian. The form is linear in its first argument. The fixed real algebra is a real form whose Killing form is negative definite. The assertion includes the zero algebra and all finite direct sums.

The form in the theorem is q(X,Y)=−BC(X,τY).(1D.1) q(X,Y)=-B_{\mathbb C}(X,\tau Y). \tag{1D.1} q(X,Y)=−BC​(X,τY).(1D.1)

Proof. We give six steps, proving both that the proposed map is well-defined and that its form is positive.

1D.1. Simple roots and generation

Assume first g≠0\mathfrak g\ne0g=0. Choose H0∈hRH_0\in\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}H0​∈hR​ with every α(H0)≠0\alpha(H_0)\ne0α(H0​)=0. 1D.6. The fixed real algebra

Let u={X:τX=X}\mathfrak u=\{X:\tau X=X\}u={X:τX=X}. It is a real Lie subalgebra. For any X∈gX\in\mathfrak gX∈g,

X=X+τX2+iX−τX2i(1D.33) X=\frac{X+\tau X}{2} +i\frac{X-\tau X}{2i} \tag{1D.33} X=2X+τX​+i2iX−τX​(1D.33)

has both displayed real components in u\mathfrak uu, and u∩iu=0\mathfrak u\cap i\mathfrak u=0u∩iu=0. Thus u⊗RC=g\mathfrak u\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C=\mathfrak gu⊗R​C=g. Equation (1D.24) makes BBB real on u\mathfrak uu, and B(X,X)=−q(X,X)<0B(X,X)=-q(X,X)<0B(X,X)=−q(X,X)<0 for nonzero X∈uX\in\mathfrak uX∈u. This restricted form is its real Killing form: the matrix of ad⁡X\operatorname{ad}XadX in a real basis of u\mathfrak uu is unchanged on complexification, so its real and complex traces agree. It is therefore the compact real form in the required algebraic sense.

Its real solvable radical is zero: a nonzero solvable real ideal would complexify to a nonzero solvable complex ideal of g\mathfrak gg. If g=0\mathfrak g=0g=0, take its unique zero-space conjugation; the Hermitian positivity assertion is vacuous and all conclusions hold.

No claim about the centre of an integrating Lie group is needed for this construction. Section 1E will use this conjugation to construct a real split triple and prove closedness in the original group, including infinite-centre groups. The algebraic construction here supplies its inner-product input.

The six steps prove Theorem 1D.1. □\square□

The simple-root and generator mechanisms are classical; compare [Etingof II], Sections 21.4 and 24.1–24.2. The diagonal-graph method is also developed in The isomorphism theorem and Serre's theorem, Section 3. We prove the triangular spanning and both graph kernels here. For the compact-form theorem itself, compare [Etingof II], Proposition 41.1. The height induction above proves positivity using the coefficient q(p+1)q(p+1)q(p+1), without invoking unitary integration or a compact-form theorem as an input.

All proof modules above allow disconnected root systems. Alternatively, for a direct sum of complex semisimple ideals, construct the maps on each ideal and take their direct sum. Cross Killing pairings vanish because the ideals commute and the adjoint products have zero trace on every summand; the Hermitian form is the sum of positive forms. This works for arbitrarily many isomorphic or nonisomorphic factors, and the zero algebra is handled as stated in Section 1D.6.

1E. A closed split rank-one subgroup in the original group

An injected Lie algebra integrates to an immersed subgroup. For the amenability argument below, the subgroup must be closed in the original group. We will prove that extra conclusion by first constructing a closed matrix image of the split triple's adjoint action, then taking the identity component of its inverse image under the original adjoint map.

Theorem 1E.1 (closed split rank-one subgroup). Every noncompact connected real Lie group with trivial connected solvable radical has a closed connected Lie subgroup locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R). No linearity, simplicity or finite-centre hypothesis is imposed on the original group.

The finite-dimensional inputs are the closed Lie subgroup theorem, the exponential charts and covering/integration results already used in Section 1C, and Cartan's criterion and the inner-derivation theorem in Symmetric spaces, Section 8. To detect noncompact directions we use Lemma 2.4 on negative Killing form and compact covers. Its proof uses homogeneous metric completeness, the bi-invariant curvature calculation and Bonnet–Myers, with its conclusions applied to the original group and its universal cover. General locally compact Lie approximation is not an input to this finite-dimensional theorem.

Proof. Let g\mathfrak gg be the Lie algebra of GGG. By Theorem 1C.5, its algebraic radical integrates to the closed connected solvable normal radical of GGG. The hypothesis therefore makes g\mathfrak gg semisimple. Write

B(X,Y)=tr⁡g(ad⁡Xad⁡Y).(1E.1) B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\operatorname{ad}X\operatorname{ad}Y). \tag{1E.1} B(X,Y)=trg​(adXadY).(1E.1)

Its complexification is semisimple by Cartan's criterion. Theorem 1D.1 supplies the compact conjugation on that complexification. We now give the real triple, its exact integrated matrix image and the closed subgroup in GGG.

The polar conjugation mechanism is classical; compare [Etingof II], Section 41.3. The formulas and signs above are checked in the present conventions.

1E.6. Lift the closed subgroup to the original group

The automorphism group of g\mathfrak gg is a closed matrix subgroup: preserving a fixed bracket tensor is a finite set of polynomial equations inside GL(g)GL(\mathfrak g)GL(g). Its Lie algebra is Der⁡g\operatorname{Der}\mathfrak gDerg, since differentiating those equations gives the derivation identity, and exponentiating a derivation preserves brackets. The existing inner-derivation proof gives

d(Ad⁡G)e=ad⁡:g→≅Lie⁡Aut⁡(g)0.(1E.28) d(\operatorname{Ad}_G)_e=\operatorname{ad}:\mathfrak g \xrightarrow{\cong}\operatorname{Lie}\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0. \tag{1E.28} d(AdG​)e​=ad:g≅​LieAut(g)0.(1E.28)

Therefore Ad⁡G:G→Aut⁡(g)0\operatorname{Ad}_G:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0AdG​:G→Aut(g)0 is a local diffeomorphism with open image. Connectedness of the target makes it onto. Its kernel is Z(G)Z(G)Z(G): an element acting trivially on the algebra commutes with every exponential, and these generate connected GGG. The kernel is discrete by (1E.28), but it need not be finite. Small identity charts and kernel translates show this surjective local isomorphism is a covering.

Now set

P=Ad⁡G−1(A1),H=P0.(1E.29) P=\operatorname{Ad}_G^{-1}(A_1),\qquad H=P^0. \tag{1E.29} P=AdG−1​(A1​),H=P0.(1E.29)

The subgroup PPP is closed by continuity, and its identity component is closed because components of a topological space are closed. Hence HHH is a closed connected embedded Lie subgroup by the exact closed-subgroup theorem. The local diffeomorphism (1E.28) identifies a neighbourhood of the identity in PPP with one in A1A_1A1​; consequently

Lie⁡H=(ad⁡)−1(Lie⁡A1)=ι(sl2(R)).(1E.30) \operatorname{Lie}H =(\operatorname{ad})^{-1}(\operatorname{Lie}A_1) =\iota(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)). \tag{1E.30} LieH=(ad)−1(LieA1​)=ι(sl2​(R)).(1E.30)

Equivalently, the exponential characterization in Theorem 1.1 proves the same preimage formula directly. The restriction H→A1H\to A_1H→A1​ has invertible derivative and open image; since A1A_1A1​ is connected it is onto, with discrete central kernel, possibly infinite. Thus HHH is locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R). This proves Theorem 1E.1 at the exact root, Lie and geometry inputs identified above. □\square□

Why each closedness step matters

An algebra inclusion alone is insufficient for closedness. In T2\mathbb T^2T2, the one-parameter subgroup t↦(eit,eiβt)t\mapsto(e^{it},e^{i\beta t})t↦(eit,eiβt), with irrational β\betaβ, is a proper dense immersed subgroup. This is a counterexample to the inference, not a counterexample to S4; its algebra is abelian. Steps 5 and 6 supply what such an integration-only argument lacks.

Likewise a complex split triple is insufficient. The complexification of su(2)\mathfrak{su}(2)su(2) is sl2(C)\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)sl2​(C), but SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) is compact and its real algebra has negative definite Killing form; it contains no real split sl2\mathfrak{sl}_2sl2​ algebra. In the present proof the real self-adjoint restricted weights and normalization (1E.16) prevent that mistake.

For the universal covering group of SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R), the adjoint image is PSL2(R)\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)PSL2​(R), but the original centre is infinite cyclic. Formula (1E.29) gives the original covering group as HHH, not an embedded copy of the matrix group. For products with compact semisimple factors, it selects the identity component of the correct preimage and excludes extra discrete central components. A group may have both compact and noncompact simple directions; the nonzero p\mathfrak pp argument needs only one noncompact direction. No finite-centre, faithful-linear-representation or simple-group assumption is imposed on GGG.

The classical subgroup statements are [Rickert], Lemmas 3.11 and 5.11. Rickert uses the adjoint-image and inverse-image strategy, with a general matrix closedness result and a nilpotent completion. Here the compatible restricted weight gives the real split triple, and two-dimensional polar factorization proves just the required matrix closedness directly. The compact-conjugation and polar-adjustment mechanisms are credited to the classical Cartan theory; compare [Etingof II], Sections 41.1 and 41.3. This proof retains the full nonlinear and infinite-centre scope.

The dual condition is B(Hα,th0)=2tB(H_\alpha,th_0)=2tB(Hα​,th0​)=2t, so Hα=h0/4H_\alpha=h_0/4Hα​=h0​/4 and d=α(Hα)=1/2d=\alpha(H_\alpha)=1/2d=α(Hα​)=1/2. Thus c=2/(4⋅1/2)=1c=\sqrt{2/(4\cdot1/2)}=1c=2/(4⋅1/2)​=1. Formula (1E.16) gives exactly e=e0e=e_0e=e0​, f=f0f=f_0f=f0​, h=h0h=h_0h=h0​. Matrix multiplication gives [e0,f0]=h0[e_0,f_0]=h_0[e0​,f0​]=h0​, [h0,e0]=2e0[h_0,e_0]=2e_0[h0​,e0​]=2e0​, [h0,f0]=−2f0[h_0,f_0]=-2f_0[h0​,f0​]=−2f0​; transposition gives θe0=−f0\theta e_0=-f_0θe0​=−f0​, θf0=−e0\theta f_0=-e_0θf0​=−e0​, θh0=−h0\theta h_0=-h_0θh0​=−h0​. Exercise 1E.2. Level 3. Let S~\widetilde SS be the simply connected covering group of SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R), and let G=S~×SU(2)G=\widetilde S\times SU(2)G=S×SU(2). Use the first-factor split algebra. Determine A1,P,HA_1,P,HA1​,P,H in (1E.29). Explain why this is a closed subgroup in the full nonlinear example, why choosing all of PPP gives the wrong connectedness statement, and why replacing GGG by SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) does not satisfy Theorem 1E.1's hypotheses.

Solution. Conjugation of the first algebra gives its adjoint group PSL2(R)\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)PSL2​(R), and the triple acts trivially on the compact factor. Thus A1=PSL2(R)×{1}A_1=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\{1\}A1​=PSL2​(R)×{1} inside the block automorphism group. The second adjoint map has kernel {I,−I}\{I,-I\}{I,−I}; the first adjoint map has discrete infinite cyclic kernel. Therefore P=S~×{I,−I}P=\widetilde S\times\{I,-I\}P=S×{I,−I}, and H=P0=S~×{I}H=P^0=\widetilde S\times\{I\}H=P0=S×{I}. The first is closed with two components; the latter is closed and connected, and its algebra is the required first-factor split algebra. Its centre is infinite cyclic. Indeed polar decomposition retracts SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R) onto the rotation circle, whose covering is R\mathbb RR; the path-class covering theorem identifies the resulting kernel with Z\mathbb ZZ, and lifting the central matrix −I-I−I gives the corresponding infinite cyclic centre of the universal cover. So replacing HHH by a finite-centre matrix subgroup would lose part of the allowed conclusion. Finally SU(2)SU(2)SU(2) is compact and has p=0\mathfrak p=0p=0; S4 requires noncompactness, so no real split triple is asserted for it.

2. Compact extensions and discrete lifts

Lemma 2.1 (compact kernel and quotient). If KKK is a compact normal subgroup and G/KG/KG/K is compact, then GGG is compact.

Proof. Choose an open identity neighborhood UUU with compact closure. The quotient map q:G→G/Kq:G\to G/Kq:G→G/K is open. Its translates q(gU)q(gU)q(gU) cover the compact quotient, so finitely many, q(giU)q(g_iU)q(gi​U), suffice. Every g∈Gg\in Gg∈G then has q(g)=q(giu)q(g)=q(g_iu)q(g)=q(gi​u) for some u∈Uu\in Uu∈U, and hence g∈giUKg\in g_iUKg∈gi​UK. Thus G=⋃i=1ngiU‾K.(2.1) G=\bigcup_{i=1}^n g_i\overline U K. \tag{2.1} G=i=1⋃n​gi​UK.(2.1) Each set on the right is compact, as a continuous image of U‾×K\overline U\times KU×K. A finite union is compact. □\square□

Lemma 2.2 (a discrete subgroup is closed). A subgroup Γ\GammaΓ of a Hausdorff topological group that is discrete in its subspace topology is closed.

Proof. Choose an identity neighborhood WWW with W∩Γ={e}W\cap\Gamma=\{e\}W∩Γ={e}, and an open identity neighborhood VVV with V−1V⊂WV^{-1}V\subset WV−1V⊂W. Every translate xVxVxV contains at most one point of Γ\GammaΓ, since two would have quotient in V−1V∩ΓV^{-1}V\cap\GammaV−1V∩Γ. If x∈Γ‾x\in\overline\Gammax∈Γ, that translate contains a point γ\gammaγ. If x≠γx\ne\gammax=γ, the open set xV∖{γ}xV\setminus\{\gamma\}xV∖{γ} contains xxx and misses Γ\GammaΓ, a contradiction. Hence x=γ∈Γx=\gamma\in\Gammax=γ∈Γ. □\square□

Lemma 2.3 (free discrete lifting). Let NNN be a closed normal subgroup of a Hausdorff topological group GGG. If G/NG/NG/N contains a subgroup Γ\GammaΓ, with its subspace topology, isomorphic to the discrete free group on rrr generators, then GGG also contains such a closed discrete subgroup.

Proof. Choose arbitrary lifts y1,…,yry_1,\ldots,y_ry1​,…,yr​ of its free generators x1,…,xrx_1,\ldots,x_rx1​,…,xr​. Let Γ~\widetilde\GammaΓ be the subgroup they generate. Any nonempty reduced relation in the yiy_iyi​'s would project to the same reduced relation in the xix_ixi​'s, which is impossible. Thus the yiy_iyi​'s freely generate Γ~\widetilde\GammaΓ, and the restricted quotient map is a bijection onto Γ\GammaΓ.

There is an open quotient identity neighborhood WWW with W∩Γ={e}W\cap\Gamma=\{e\}W∩Γ={e}. Its inverse image meets Γ~\widetilde\GammaΓ only in the identity. Translating this neighborhood shows that Γ~\widetilde\GammaΓ is discrete in GGG; Lemma 2.2 makes it closed. These arguments also show that the restriction is a topological isomorphism of discrete groups. □\square□

This lifting statement uses freeness. Arbitrary lifts of generators of a group with relations need not satisfy those relations. It also uses the discrete subgroup topology, rather than just injectivity of an abstract homomorphism.

3. Two explicit matrices and the free subgroup

Consider the determinant-one matrices A=(1301),B=(1031).(3.1) A=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{3.1} A=(10​31​),B=(13​01​).(3.1) On the real projective line R∪{∞}\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}R∪{∞}, their nonzero integer powers act by Anx=x+3n,Bnx=x3nx+1,Bn∞=13n.(3.2) A^nx=x+3n,\qquad B^nx=\frac{x}{3nx+1},\qquad B^n\infty=\frac1{3n}. \tag{3.2} Anx=x+3n,Bnx=3nx+1x​,Bn∞=3n1​.(3.2) Put X={x∈R:∣x∣>1}∪{∞},Y={x∈R:∣x∣<1}.(3.3) X=\{x\in\mathbb R:|x|>1\}\cup\{\infty\}, \qquad Y=\{x\in\mathbb R:|x|<1\}. \tag{3.3} X={x∈R:∣x∣>1}∪{∞},Y={x∈R:∣x∣<1}.(3.3)

We can check every reduced word without a separate ping-pong convention. Write it as alternating nonzero power blocks of AAA and BBB. Apply the rightmost block to 111, a point outside both XXX and YYY. Its image is in XXX for an AAA-block, since ∣1+3n∣≥2|1+3n|\geq2∣1+3n∣≥2; it is in YYY for a BBB-block, since ∣3n+1∣≥2|3n+1|\geq2∣3n+1∣≥2. All these matrices have integer entries. An entrywise neighborhood of III of radius less than 1/21/21/2 contains no other integer matrix, so their matrix subgroup is discrete. For the projective subgroup, use a sufficiently small symmetric neighborhood VVV of III, with VVV containing no other integer matrix and V∩(−V)=∅V\cap(-V)=\varnothingV∩(−V)=∅. The quotient by {±I}\{\pm I\}{±I} is open, and the inverse image of its image of VVV is V∪(−V)V\cup(-V)V∪(−V). Its integer points are only I,−II,-II,−I, both representing the projective identity. The projective subgroup is discrete as well. Lemma 2.2 proves closedness in both groups. □\square□

Corollary 3.2. Every connected Lie group HHH locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R) contains a closed discrete copy of F2F_2F2​.

Proof. Its quotient by the closed center is PSL2(R)\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)PSL2​(R), by the adjoint correspondence stated in Section 1. Apply Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 2.3. An infinite discrete center causes no difficulty for that lifting lemma. □\square□

In particular SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R) is not amenable: amenability would pass to its closed discrete F2F_2F2​, contradicting the complete reduced-word mean calculation in the discrete lesson.

The source's alternative reduced-word calculation can also be checked directly. Then S∪aSa−1=F2∖{e},bnSb−n∩bmSb−m=∅(n≠m).(3.5) S\cup aSa^{-1}=F_2\setminus\{e\},\qquad b^nSb^{-n}\cap b^mSb^{-m}=\varnothing\quad(n\ne m). \tag{3.5} S∪aSa−1=F2​∖{e},bnSb−n∩bmSb−m=∅(n=m).(3.5) For the first identity, a nonidentity word outside SSS begins with a bbb-block; conjugating it by a−1a^{-1}a−1 gives a word in SSS. 4. The full almost-connected criterion

Proposition 4.1 (the semisimple obstruction). A noncompact almost-connected semisimple locally compact group SSS contains a closed discrete subgroup topologically isomorphic to F2F_2F2​.

Proof. Its identity component S∘S^\circS∘ is semisimple by Lemma 1.1, and is noncompact: otherwise compactness of S/S∘S/S^\circS/S∘ and Lemma 2.1 would make SSS compact. Use S2 to choose compact normal K⊂S∘K\subset S^\circK⊂S∘ with connected Lie quotient L=S∘/K.(4.1) L=S^\circ/K. \tag{4.1} L=S∘/K.(4.1) Theorem 1A.10 makes LLL semisimple. It is noncompact by Lemma 2.1 again. Input S4 supplies a closed connected subgroup H⊂LH\subset LH⊂L locally isomorphic to SL2(R)\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)SL2​(R). Corollary 3.2 supplies a closed discrete F2F_2F2​ in HHH, and hence in LLL, since HHH is closed with its subgroup topology.

Lemma 2.3 lifts it through S∘→LS^\circ\to LS∘→L to a closed discrete subgroup of S∘S^\circS∘. The latter is closed in SSS, so the lifted subgroup is also closed in SSS and has the same discrete topology. □\square□

Theorem 4.2 (amenability and the radical). Let GGG be an almost-connected locally compact Hausdorff group and R=rad⁡GR=\operatorname{rad}GR=radG. The following are equivalent:

  1. GGG is amenable.
  2. G/RG/RG/R is compact.
  3. GGG has no closed discrete subgroup topologically isomorphic to F2F_2F2​.

Proof. If G/RG/RG/R is compact, it is amenable by normalized Haar measure. The closed solvable subgroup RRR is amenable by Proposition 6.1 of the Haar lesson, using its finite closed derived series. The normal-extension theorem gives amenability of GGG. Thus 2 implies 1.

If GGG is amenable, its closed subgroups are amenable by Theorem 2.1 of the continuous averaging lesson. A discrete F2F_2F2​ is not amenable, so 1 implies 3.

If G/RG/RG/R is noncompact, Lemma 1.1 makes it an almost-connected semisimple locally compact group. Proposition 4.1 produces a closed discrete F2F_2F2​ in G/RG/RG/R, and Lemma 2.3 lifts it to one in GGG. This contradicts 3, proving 3 implies 2. □\square□

Only the implication from a noncompact quotient to a free subgroup uses the almost-connected hypothesis. The implication from compact G/RG/RG/R to amenability holds for any locally compact GGG. In fact a compact G/RG/RG/R already makes GGG almost connected, since R⊂G∘R\subset G^\circR⊂G∘ and G/G∘G/G^\circG/G∘ is its continuous quotient.
