5. Solvable matrices and a non-Lie example

Example 5.1 (triangular groups over a locally compact field). Let kkk be a commutative locally compact Hausdorff topological field. The group Tn(k)T_n(k)Tn​(k) of invertible upper triangular matrices is a closed subgroup of the locally compact group GLn(k)\mathrm{GL}_n(k)GLn​(k). Indeed the determinant-nonzero set is open in kn2k^{n^2}kn2, matrix multiplication and inversion are continuous, and the lower-entry zero equations define a closed subset relative to that set. The diagonal homomorphism maps Tn(k)T_n(k)Tn​(k) to the abelian group (k×)n(k^\times)^n(k×)n, with kernel N=1+JN=1+JN=1+J, where JJJ is the algebra of strictly upper triangular matrices.

The powers of this algebra satisfy Jn=0J^n=0Jn=0. In the quotient algebra modulo Jp+qJ^{p+q}Jp+q, matrices 1+u1+u1+u and 1+v1+v1+v, for u∈Jp,v∈Jqu\in J^p,v\in J^qu∈Jp,v∈Jq, commute, since both cross-products vanish. Their inverses are finite geometric sums. Therefore [1+Jp,1+Jq]⊂1+Jp+q,Dr(N)⊂1+J2r.(5.1) [1+J^p,1+J^q]\subset 1+J^{p+q}, \qquad D^r(N)\subset 1+J^{2^r}. \tag{5.1} [1+Jp,1+Jq]⊂1+Jp+q,Dr(N)⊂1+J2r.(5.1) Here DrD^rDr denotes the algebraic derived subgroup. For 2r≥n2^r\geq n2r≥n, it is trivial. The first derived subgroup of Tn(k)T_n(k)Tn​(k) is in NNN, so a derived-length bound for Tn(k)T_n(k)Tn​(k) is 1+⌈log⁡2n⌉.(5.2) 1+\lceil\log_2 n\rceil. \tag{5.2} 1+⌈log2​n⌉.(5.2) This includes n=1n=1n=1, where the group is abelian. Thus these groups are solvable and amenable at their given locally compact topology. Conjugation by the matrix reversing the coordinate order gives the same conclusion for lower triangular groups. The argument works for R,C\mathbb R,\mathbb CR,C, the ppp-adic fields, and discrete fields. In particular the source's rational-field example may use Q\mathbb QQ with the discrete topology; its usual topology inherited from R\mathbb RR is not locally compact. A compact rational neighborhood in that topology would also be compact and closed in R\mathbb RR, yet would contain all rationals in an interval about its center. An irrational point in that interval is a real limit of those rationals, contradicting closedness.

Example 5.2 (compact semisimple factors without a Lie quotient assumption on GGG). Put C=∏j=1∞SO(3),G=R×C,R=R×{e}.(5.3) C=\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{SO}(3),\qquad G=\mathbb R\times C,\qquad R=\mathbb R\times\{e\}. \tag{5.3} C=j=1∏∞​SO(3),G=R×C,R=R×{e}.(5.3) The product CCC is compact by product compactness and connected: finite-support elements form a dense connected union of the connected finite products. Thus GGG is connected and locally compact.

We verify that the displayed RRR really is the radical. The Lie algebra of SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) is R3\mathbb R^3R3 with the cross-product bracket. A nonzero ideal containing v≠0v\ne0v=0 contains every w×vw\times vw×v, hence v⊥v^\perpv⊥ as well as vvv, and therefore the whole algebra. It is simple and nonabelian; its brackets span the whole algebra, so it is not solvable. By the closed-subgroup Lie correspondence, a closed connected solvable normal subgroup of SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) must have zero Lie algebra and be trivial.

For any connected solvable normal subgroup PPP of GGG, the closure of each projection of PPP onto an SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) coordinate is connected, solvable and normal. The closure solvability argument following Lemma 1.1 applies. Every such projection is therefore trivial. Hence P⊂RP\subset RP⊂R. Since RRR itself is connected, abelian and normal, it is the radical. The quotient G/R=CG/R=CG/R=C is compact, so Theorem 4.2 proves amenability of GGG.

This group is not a finite-dimensional Lie group. Such Lie groups have an identity neighborhood containing no nontrivial subgroup. To see this, choose a norm on the Lie algebra and an exponential chart injective on the ball of radius 2ε2\varepsilon2ε. Inside the image of the ball of radius ε\varepsilonε, a nonidentity exp⁡X\exp XexpX has some power exp⁡(2mX)\exp(2^mX)exp(2mX) whose norm lies in [ε,2ε)[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon)[ε,2ε), so that power lies outside the smaller neighborhood. Injectivity in the larger chart justifies this comparison.

In contrast, every identity neighborhood in GGG contains a basic product neighborhood restricting only finitely many SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) coordinates. An unrestricted coordinate contributes its entire nontrivial subgroup. Thus GGG fails this Lie neighborhood property. Its amenability is a case of the full locally compact criterion, not just a conclusion about a Lie group.

Example 5.3 (the positive affine group). The matrices (ab01),a>0,b∈R,(5.4) \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a>0,\quad b\in\mathbb R, \tag{5.4} (a0​b1​),a>0,b∈R,(5.4) form a connected solvable group. Its radical is the whole group, so its radical quotient is trivial and compact. It is amenable even though it is noncompact and nonunimodular. The Haar density a−2 da dba^{-2}\,da\,dba−2dadb and subgroup averaging normalization were checked in the preceding two lessons.

The remaining examples in Takesaki's Example XIII.4.4 follow from those same full permanence proofs: an increasing union of closed amenable subgroups is amenable; a discrete directed union of finite groups is such a union; and the finite-support permutation group is the union of its finite symmetric groups. More generally, any locally compact Hausdorff topology on a directed union of finite subgroups allows the same argument, since finite subgroups are closed and compact. Every compact group has its normalized Haar mean. Every discrete FnF_nFn​, n≥2n\geq2n≥2, contains the closed F2F_2F2​ generated by its first two generators and is nonamenable. No additional hypothesis about countability of the ambient locally compact group is needed for these applications.

The increasing-union proof can give a two-sided mean as well. Choose a two-sided mean mim_imi​ on each subgroup's UC(Hi)\mathrm{UC}(H_i)UC(Hi​), using Proposition 2.2 of the Haar lesson, and define Mi(f)=mi(f∣Hi)M_i(f)=m_i(f|_{H_i})Mi​(f)=mi​(f∣Hi​​) on UC(G)\mathrm{UC}(G)UC(G). Restriction preserves both forms of uniform continuity. For each g∈Gg\in Gg∈G, all sufficiently late subgroups contain ggg, and both Mi(Lgf)=Mi(f)M_i(L_gf)=M_i(f)Mi​(Lg​f)=Mi​(f) and Mi(Rgf)=Mi(f)M_i(R_gf)=M_i(f)Mi​(Rg​f)=Mi​(f) then hold. A weak-star convergent subnet of the states MiM_iMi​ has a two-sided invariant limit. The extension argument in that same Proposition 2.2 gives a two-sided Haar L∞(G)L^\infty(G)L∞(G) mean. This checks the source's right-invariance observation as well as its amenability conclusion.

6. Exercises with solutions

Level 1 asks for a computation or a direct application. Level 2 asks for a proof using the lesson’s framework. Level 3 combines results or examines a hypothesis whose failure changes the conclusion.

Exercise 6.1 (the projective boundary point). Level 1. For n≠0n\ne0n=0, compute An1,Bn1,Bn∞A^n1,B^n1,B^n\inftyAn1,Bn1,Bn∞. Check their domains, including n=−1n=-1n=−1, and explain why the point 111 detects every nonempty reduced power-block word.

Solution. The values are 1+3n1+3n1+3n, 1/(3n+1)1/(3n+1)1/(3n+1), and 1/(3n)1/(3n)1/(3n). Their absolute values are respectively at least 222, at most 1/21/21/2, and at most 1/31/31/3, so they lie in X,Y,YX,Y,YX,Y,Y. For n=−1n=-1n=−1 they are −2,−1/2,−1/3-2,-1/2,-1/3−2,−1/2,−1/3. The rightmost block sends 111 into its prescribed domain. Alternating blocks then switch the domain using (3.4) and AnY⊂XA^nY\subset XAnY⊂X. The final value is in X∪YX\cup YX∪Y, which excludes 111. Thus neither projective identity nor a matrix scalar ±I\pm I±I can be a nonempty reduced word.

Exercise 6.2 (the kernel need not be compact). Level 2. If q:G→G/Nq:G\to G/Nq:G→G/N is a group quotient with NNN closed, and the quotient contains a discrete F2F_2F2​, prove that arbitrary lifts of its generators give a closed discrete F2F_2F2​ even when NNN is infinite and noncompact. Where would the argument fail for two commuting quotient generators?

Solution. A reduced relation among the lifts would project to a reduced relation in F2F_2F2​, so the restriction is injective. A quotient neighborhood isolating the identity of F2F_2F2​ pulls back to a neighborhood isolating the identity of the lifted subgroup. Translations give discreteness and Lemma 2.2 gives closedness. Neither step bounds the kernel. For commuting generators the quotient word xyx−1y−1xyx^{-1}y^{-1}xyx−1y−1 is already trivial, so projecting a relation does not exclude that relation, and lifting may instead give a nontrivial commutator in NNN. A free-group lift is ensured by the absence of relations.

Exercise 6.3 (why both compactness assumptions matter). Level 2. Prove that a noncompact group with a compact normal subgroup cannot have compact quotient. Give examples showing that compactness of the kernel alone, or of the quotient alone, does not imply compactness of the group.

Solution. The first assertion is the contrapositive of Lemma 2.1, whose finite cover by giU‾Kg_i\overline U Kgi​UK proves compactness if both are compact. For kernel alone take R\mathbb RR with kernel {0}\{0\}{0}; its quotient is noncompact. For quotient alone take R\mathbb RR with kernel R\mathbb RR; the quotient is trivial. These are closed normal subgroups, so the examples respect the quotient hypotheses.

Exercise 6.4 (the Euclidean motion radical). Level 3. Let E=R3⋊SO(3)E=\mathbb R^3\rtimes\mathrm{SO}(3)E=R3⋊SO(3), with multiplication (v,Q)(w,P)=(v+Qw,QP)(v,Q)(w,P)=(v+Qw,QP)(v,Q)(w,P)=(v+Qw,QP). Determine its radical and prove amenability. Is EEE solvable?

Solution. The translation subgroup V=R3×{I}V=\mathbb R^3\times\{I\}V=R3×{I} is closed, connected, abelian and normal. A connected solvable normal subgroup of EEE has connected solvable normal image closure in SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3), which is trivial by the Lie-algebra argument of Example 5.2. Thus every such subgroup is contained in VVV, and rad⁡E=V\operatorname{rad}E=VradE=V. The group is connected, its quotient by VVV is compact, and Theorem 4.2 gives amenability. It is not solvable, since its quotient SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) has a non-solvable Lie algebra. A solvable group would have a solvable quotient and Lie algebra.

Exercise 6.5 (triangular derived length). Level 1. Give the bound (5.2) for n=1,3,4,5n=1,3,4,5n=1,3,4,5. Why is it valid in characteristic two as well?

Solution. The bounds are 1,3,3,41,3,3,41,3,3,4. The filtration argument uses Jn=0J^n=0Jn=0, the ideal products JpJq⊂Jp+qJ^pJ^q\subset J^{p+q}JpJq⊂Jp+q, finite geometric inverses, and commutation in a quotient algebra. It never divides by two or uses a characteristic-zero Lie bracket. Thus it remains valid over a field of characteristic two. The bound need not be claimed minimal.

Exercise 6.6 (an infinite compact product). Level 2. In Example 5.2, prove density and connectedness of the finite-support union. Use it to establish connectedness of GGG, and prove the failure of the Lie neighborhood property without using a dimension count.

Solution. Let CnC_nCn​ be the product with identity in every coordinate after nnn. It is connected, the CnC_nCn​'s are increasing and share the identity, so their union is connected: a separation would separate one of the CnC_nCn​'s containing a point from each part. Every basic product open set restricts finitely many coordinates, which can be matched by an element of some CnC_nCn​; hence the union is dense. Its closure CCC is connected. The product of the connected spaces R\mathbb RR and CCC is connected. Every identity neighborhood contains a basic one restricting finitely many coordinates, so it contains a full untouched SO(3)\mathrm{SO}(3)SO(3) coordinate subgroup. The exponential-chart argument of Example 5.2 excludes this in a finite-dimensional Lie group, proving that GGG is not Lie.

Exercise 6.7 (the almost-connected hypothesis). Level 3. Show that the discrete additive group Z\mathbb ZZ is amenable and has trivial connected radical, but its radical quotient is noncompact. Identify exactly which step of Proposition 4.1 cannot be applied.

Solution. The discrete group is abelian and therefore amenable. Its identity component is {0}\{0\}{0}, so every connected subgroup is trivial and rad⁡Z={0}\operatorname{rad}\mathbb Z=\{0\}radZ={0}. Its radical quotient is the infinite discrete group Z\mathbb ZZ, which is noncompact: the singleton open cover has no finite subcover. It is not almost connected. In Proposition 4.1 the deduction that a noncompact SSS has noncompact S∘S^\circS∘ used compactness of S/S∘S/S^\circS/S∘. Here S∘S^\circS∘ is compact and S/S∘S/S^\circS/S∘ is not. There is no noncompact connected semisimple Lie quotient to which S4 could be applied.

Exercise 6.8 (why “discrete subgroup” is essential). Level 3. Reconcile the equivalence in Theorem 4.2 with the existence of a continuous injective homomorphism from discrete F2F_2F2​ into a compact group. Use the finite permutation construction in Exercise 4.4 of the continuous averaging lesson, and check the identity neighborhoods of the image.

Solution. That construction gives homomorphisms separating all nonidentity reduced words in finite symmetric groups. Their product is injective into a compact product, and its image closure CCC is compact and amenable. The map is continuous because its domain is discrete. Every product identity neighborhood contains the kernel of a finite list of finite quotient maps. That kernel has finite index in the infinite group F2F_2F2​ and contains a nonidentity element. Thus the image is not discrete in its subspace topology. It cannot be a closed image either: its countable infinite closure would contradict the Baire theorem, since a compact Hausdorff group that is countable has an open singleton and is consequently finite. Theorem 4.2 forbids a closed discrete topological copy of F2F_2F2​, so this dense image gives no contradiction. The source's free-subgroup convention is precisely the discrete subgroup convention.

JZJ−1=−Z. Thus ZZZ commutes with every element of the zero Lie algebra, but it does not commute with the nonidentity element of LLL.

Write a matrix u∈U(2)u\in U(2)u∈U(2) as u=(uij)u=(u_{ij})u=(uij​). The equation uJ=JuuJ=JuuJ=Ju forces u12=u21=0u_{12}=u_{21}=0u12​=u21​=0. Consequently N∘=C∘=C,L∘C∘=C, N^\circ=C^\circ=C, \qquad L^\circ C^\circ=C, N∘=C∘=C,L∘C∘=C, and n=c={diag⁡(iα,iβ):α,β∈R}. \mathfrak n=\mathfrak c =\{\operatorname{diag}(i\alpha,i\beta):\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\}. n=c={diag(iα,iβ):α,β∈R}. In particular Z∉nZ\notin\mathfrak nZ∈/n and Z∉cZ\notin\mathfrak cZ∈/c.

Since Z2=−IZ^2=-IZ2=−I, its exponential is exp⁡(tZ)=(cos⁡tsin⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t). \exp(tZ)= \begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}. exp(tZ)=(cost−sint​sintcost​). If the whole one-parameter group normalized LLL, this commutator curve would lie in LLL, and its derivative would have to lie in l={0}\mathfrak l=\{0\}l={0}, which is impossible.

The missing step is therefore a group-level condition. In Lemma 1A.2 the orthogonal remainder has both [Z,l]=0[Z,\mathfrak l]=0[Z,l]=0 and Z∈nZ\in\mathfrak nZ∈n. Exercise 6.10 (the solvable lift and its finite bound). Level 2. Let GGG be connected and locally compact Hausdorff, let K⊲GK\lhd GK⊲G be compact, and write q:G→G/Kq:G\to G/Kq:G→G/K. Let PPP be a closed connected normal subgroup of G/KG/KG/K, with DdP={e}D^dP=\{e\}DdP={e} for some finite integer d≥0d\geq0d≥0. Here D0A=AD^0A=AD0A=A and Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA]D^{j+1}A=[D^jA,D^jA]Dj+1A=[DjA,DjA] are algebraic derived subgroups. Put C=CG(K),A=Z(K), C=C_G(K),\qquad A=Z(K), C=CG​(K),A=Z(K), and E=C∩q−1(P). E=C\cap q^{-1}(P). E=C∩q−1(P). Use Theorem 1A.4 and Theorem 1A.9 to prove that E∘E^\circE∘ is a connected solvable subgroup normal in GGG, and that it maps onto PPP. Establish the explicit bound DdE⊂A,Dd+1E={e}. D^dE\subset A, \qquad D^{d+1}E=\{e\}. DdE⊂A,Dd+1E={e}. Deduce Theorem 1A.10 when GGG has no nontrivial connected solvable normal subgroup. Explain how to handle a connected solvable normal PPP that is not closed, without losing its finite derived-length bound.

Solution. Theorem 1A.4 gives G=KCG=KCG=KC and the topological identification C/A≅G/K. C/A\cong G/K. C/A≅G/K. Indeed C∩K=Z(K)=AC\cap K=Z(K)=AC∩K=Z(K)=A. The resulting map qC:C→G/Kq_C:C\to G/KqC​:C→G/K is an open surjection with compact kernel AAA. The kernel is central in CCC, since every element of CCC commutes with all of KKK; in particular AAA is abelian.

The centralizer CCC is closed: its commuting equations are closed equations in the Hausdorff group GGG. It is normal in GGG, because conjugation preserves the normal subgroup KKK. The group q−1(P)q^{-1}(P)q−1(P) is also closed and normal. Thus EEE is closed, locally compact Hausdorff, and normal in GGG.

The restriction qE:E→Pq_E:E\to PqE​:E→P is onto, because qCq_CqC​ is onto and EEE is the full preimage of PPP within CCC. It has kernel AAA. To check its topology, an open set in EEE has the form O∩EO\cap EO∩E, with OOO open in CCC, and qE(O∩E)=qC(O)∩P. q_E(O\cap E)=q_C(O)\cap P. qE​(O∩E)=qC​(O)∩P. The right side is open in the subgroup topology of PPP. Hence qEq_EqE​ is an open quotient map, and E/A≅PE/A\cong PE/A≅P as topological groups.

A surjective homomorphism takes a derived subgroup onto the derived subgroup of its image: every image commutator is the image of a commutator of lifts, and the same holds for the subgroups they generate. Induction gives qE(DjE)=DjP(j≥0). q_E(D^jE)=D^jP \quad(j\geq0). qE​(DjE)=DjP(j≥0). At step ddd this image is trivial, so DdE⊂AD^dE\subset ADdE⊂A. Since AAA is abelian, taking one more derived subgroup gives Dd+1E={e}D^{d+1}E=\{e\}Dd+1E={e}. This is a finite algebraic bound. It remains valid for d=0d=0d=0: then P={e}P=\{e\}P={e}, E=AE=AE=A, and D1E={e}D^1E=\{e\}D1E={e}. The bound need not be minimal.

Every continuous automorphism of EEE preserves the component containing the identity. Since conjugation by each element of GGG restricts to such an automorphism, E∘⊲GE^\circ\lhd GE∘⊲G. It is connected by definition, and it is solvable because its derived series is contained termwise in that of EEE. Apply Theorem 1A.9 to the compact-kernel quotient E→E/A≅PE\to E/A\cong PE→E/A≅P. It gives qE(E∘)=P∘=P. q_E(E^\circ)=P^\circ=P. qE​(E∘)=P∘=P. Thus E∘E^\circE∘ is the required normal connected solvable lift. If GGG contains no nontrivial subgroup with these three properties, then E∘={e}E^\circ=\{e\}E∘={e}, so its surjective image PPP is trivial.

For a possibly nonclosed PPP, first replace it by P‾\overline PP in G/KG/KG/K. Closure preserves connectedness. It also preserves normality, because each conjugation map is a homeomorphism. To check solvability, closure of a subgroup is a subgroup, and continuity of the commutator map gives [B‾,B‾]⊂[B,B]‾ [\overline B,\overline B] \subset\overline{[B,B]} [B,B]⊂[B,B]​ for every subgroup BBB: approximate each pair by pairs from BBB, then use that the closed subgroup on the right contains the resulting commutators and their generated subgroup. Induction yields Dj(P‾)⊂DjP‾. D^j(\overline P)\subset\overline{D^jP}. Dj(P)⊂DjP. Therefore Dd(P‾)={e}D^d(\overline P)=\{e\}Dd(P)={e}. The preceding lift argument applies to this closed subgroup and forces P‾={e}\overline P=\{e\}P={e}, hence P={e}P=\{e\}P={e}. Its connected lift maps onto P‾\overline PP; no local compactness of the original nonclosed subgroup is being assumed.

Exercise 6.11 (a dense component image through a noncompact kernel). Level 3. Define the additive group of compatible binary residues by Z2=lim←⁡m≥1Z/2mZ. \mathbb Z_2= \varprojlim_{m\geq1}\mathbb Z/2^m\mathbb Z. Z2​=m≥1lim​​Z/2mZ. Concretely, an element is a sequence (am)(a_m)(am​) of residues such that reduction of am+1a_{m+1}am+1​ modulo 2m2^m2m is ama_mam​. Give it coordinatewise addition and the topology in which prescribing one residue ama_mam​ is a basic open condition. Write n^\widehat nn for the compatible residues of an integer nnn. Put H=R×Z2, H=\mathbb R\times\mathbb Z_2, H=R×Z2​, and N={(n,n^):n∈Z}, N=\{(n,\widehat n):n\in\mathbb Z\}, N={(n,n):n∈Z}, with the product topology on HHH, and give H/NH/NH/N the group quotient topology.

Prove directly that Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ is compact Hausdorff and totally disconnected, with Z^\widehat{\mathbb Z}Z dense and proper. Prove that HHH is locally compact Hausdorff, that NNN is closed, discrete and noncompact, and that H∘=R×{0}H^\circ=\mathbb R\times\{0\}H∘=R×{0}. Show that H/NH/NH/N is compact and connected, while the image of H∘H^\circH∘ is dense and proper. Identify exactly where the proof of Theorem 1A.9 needs compactness of its kernel.

Solution. Let πm:Z2→Z/2mZ\pi_m:\mathbb Z_2\to\mathbb Z/2^m\mathbb Zπm​:Z2​→Z/2mZ be the residue projection. The sets Um(a)={x:πm(x)=a} U_m(a)=\{x:\pi_m(x)=a\} Um​(a)={x:πm​(x)=a} are open and closed. They form a basis because finitely many compatible coordinate conditions reduce to the condition at their largest index. Distinct elements differ in some coordinate, whose disjoint cylinders separate them. Thus the topology is Hausdorff. Addition and inversion are continuous because every finite residue group has the discrete group topology and these operations respect the projections.

Here is a direct compactness proof. Each cylinder at level mmm is the disjoint union of its two cylinders at level m+1m+1m+1; each is nonempty, since an integer representing its prescribed residue supplies a compatible element. Suppose an open cover of Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ had no finite subcover. Begin with the whole space at level zero. At each level choose a child cylinder having no finite subcover from the given cover; at least one child has this property, since the union of two finite subcovers would cover its parent. The chosen residues are compatible and define an element xxx. A cover member containing xxx contains some basic cylinder Um(πm(x))U_m(\pi_m(x))Um​(πm​(x)). That is exactly the chosen cylinder at level mmm, and this one cover member covers it, a contradiction. Therefore Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ is compact.

A connected subset has a singleton image under every πm\pi_mπm​, since a finite discrete space has no larger connected subset. All its coordinates are consequently fixed, so the subset has at most one point. This proves total disconnectedness. The map n↦n^n\mapsto\widehat nn↦n is injective: an integer divisible by every 2m2^m2m is zero. Its image is dense because every cylinder contains a representing integer.

To see that the image is proper, choose the compatible element zzz with residues πm(z)=∑0≤2j<m22j(mod2m). \pi_m(z)= \sum_{0\leq2j<m}2^{2j}\pmod{2^m}. πm​(z)=0≤2j<m∑​22j(mod2m). Compatibility follows because any added term vanishes on reduction to the previous modulus. If kkk is the number of terms in this finite sum, then 2k≥m2k\geq m2k≥m, and 3∑j=0k−14j=4k−1≡−1(mod2m). 3\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}4^j=4^k-1 \equiv-1\pmod{2^m}. 3j=0∑k−1​4j=4k−1≡−1(mod2m). Hence 3z=−1^3z=-\widehat13z=−1. If z=n^z=\widehat nz=n for an integer nnn, then 3n+13n+13n+1 would be divisible by every 2m2^m2m, so 3n+1=03n+1=03n+1=0 as an integer, which is impossible. Thus z∉Z^z\notin\widehat{\mathbb Z}z∈/Z.

The product HHH is Hausdorff and locally compact: around (r,x)(r,x)(r,x), the product [r−1,r+1]×Z2[r-1,r+1]\times\mathbb Z_2[r−1,r+1]×Z2​ is a compact neighborhood. It is abelian, so NNN is normal. The neighborhood (−1/2,1/2)×Z2 (-1/2,1/2)\times\mathbb Z_2 (−1/2,1/2)×Z2​ meets NNN only at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Translation shows that NNN is discrete. It is also closed. If r∉Zr\notin\mathbb Zr∈/Z, choose a real neighborhood of rrr missing Z\mathbb ZZ. If r=n∈Zr=n\in\mathbb Zr=n∈Z but x≠n^x\ne\widehat nx=n, choose a cylinder neighborhood of xxx missing n^\widehat nn, and take its product with (n−1/2,n+1/2)(n-1/2,n+1/2)(n−1/2,n+1/2). These neighborhoods miss NNN and cover every point outside it. Finally NNN is noncompact: its continuous first projection is the unbounded subset Z\mathbb ZZ of R\mathbb RR, whereas a compact subset of R\mathbb RR is bounded.

The projection of any connected subset of HHH into Z2\mathbb Z_2Z2​ is a singleton. Thus the identity component is contained in R×{0}\mathbb R\times\{0\}R×{0}. That subgroup is connected and contains the identity, so H∘=R×{0}. H^\circ=\mathbb R\times\{0\}. H∘=R×{0}.

Let q:H→Y=H/Nq:H\to Y=H/Nq:H→Y=H/N be the actual quotient map. It is open, since for open O⊂HO\subset HO⊂H its saturation O+NO+NO+N is a union of translates of OOO. Since NNN is closed, the Hausdorff quotient fact proved before Theorem 1A.9 applies. In particular YYY is a Hausdorff topological group, with precisely this quotient topology.

Every (r,x)∈H(r,x)\in H(r,x)∈H has the same coset as (r−n,x−n^) (r-n,x-\widehat n) (r−n,x−n) for any integer nnn. Choose nnn with 0≤r−n<10\leq r-n<10≤r−n<1. This proves that q([0,1]×Z2)=Y. q([0,1]\times\mathbb Z_2)=Y. q([0,1]×Z2​)=Y. The set on the left is a continuous image of a compact set. Hence YYY is compact, and in particular locally compact Hausdorff.

Set M=q(H∘)M=q(H^\circ)M=q(H∘). It is connected as the continuous image of R\mathbb RR. For any (r,x)∈H(r,x)\in H(r,x)∈H, choose integers nmn_mnm​ representing πm(x)\pi_m(x)πm​(x). Then n^m→x\widehat n_m\to xnm​→x, since each fixed residue agrees for all sufficiently large mmm. Consequently q(r,n^m)⟶q(r,x). q(r,\widehat n_m)\longrightarrow q(r,x). q(r,nm​)⟶q(r,x). But q(r,n^m)=q(r−nm,0)∈Mq(r,\widehat n_m)=q(r-n_m,0)\in Mq(r,nm​)=q(r−nm​,0)∈M. Thus MMM is dense in YYY. Closure preserves connectedness, so Y=M‾Y=\overline MY=M is connected and Y∘=YY^\circ=YY∘=Y.

The image MMM is proper. For the element zzz constructed above, an equality q(0,z)=q(t,0)q(0,z)=q(t,0)q(0,z)=q(t,0) would imply (−t,z)=(n,n^) (-t,z)=(n,\widehat n) (−t,z)=(n,n) for some integer nnn, contradicting z∉Z^z\notin\widehat{\mathbb Z}z∈/Z. Therefore q(H∘)=M≠Y∘,M‾=Y. q(H^\circ)=M\ne Y^\circ, \qquad \overline M=Y. q(H∘)=M=Y∘,M=Y.

Theorem 1A.9 uses a compact kernel to ensure that the product H∘NH^\circ NH∘N is closed, equivalently that q(H∘)q(H^\circ)q(H∘) is closed. Here that product is H∘N=R×Z^, H^\circ N=\mathbb R\times\widehat{\mathbb Z}, H∘N=R×Z, which is dense and proper in HHH. The same failure appears after passing to H/H∘≅Z2H/H^\circ\cong\mathbb Z_2H/H∘≅Z2​: the image of NNN is Z^\widehat{\mathbb Z}Z, which is not closed. Corollary 1A.8 about Hausdorff quotients of totally disconnected locally compact groups requires a closed normal subgroup, so it cannot be applied to this image. The original group HHH itself has a nontrivial connected component; the example makes no claim that a Hausdorff quotient of a totally disconnected locally compact group can become connected.

This construction is an explicit case of the classical diagonal-lattice mechanism in Rickert, Theorem 2.2, printed page 435. All facts needed for this case have been proved above.
